claims.claim: AI will need so much energy we have to burn more fossil fuels to keep up
heard_as: AI will make emissions explode
We can't decarbonise while running AI
ChatGPT is destroying the climate
AI is a fossil fuel technology
We need to burn more gas to power AI
Nuclear is the only way to run AI
Data centres will consume half the grid
claims.kernel: The numbers being thrown around sound enormous, and the tech companies themselves act as if the worry is real. They are signing gas deals, restarting nuclear plants and buying up grid connections. Every week there's a story about a giant data centre that needs a whole reactor. If your reference point is Meta buying 10 gas plants to power a single Louisiana data centre, "AI is a fossil fuel problem" looks like a plain description of what's happening.
claims.truth: The real picture is smaller and easier to manage than the news coverage suggests. - Data centres use **around 1 to 3% of world electricity** today, AI included. - The often-quoted line that "AI search uses 10× the energy of a Google search" came from Alphabet's chairman in 2023. Tech companies have not published real numbers to check it since. - The IEA expects world electricity demand to grow by about 6,000 TWh by 2030. Data centres account for only about 3% of that growth. - Industry, buildings, electric vehicles, air conditioning and heating, in that order, each add more to the 2023-2030 increase than data centres do. - Even if AI demand doubles or triples, data centres reach about 6% of global electricity. - Location matters more than the global total. In Ireland, data centres use 17% of national electricity, and in more than five US states they use at least 10%. That is a real problem for local grids and planning, rather than for global emissions. - Personal AI use is tiny: 100 ChatGPT questions use about as much energy as streaming a 20-minute video, or running an electric heater for one minute. - We have been here before. In the late 1990s, people predicted data centres would eat over half of US electricity. Between 2010 and 2018, global computing grew 550% while data centre energy use grew only 6%, thanks to steady efficiency gains known as Koomey's Law.
claims.say_this: AI will use more electricity, but much less than the news stories suggest: data centres are about 1 to 3% of world electricity, and even gloomy forecasts only take that to around 6%. Tech firms are building gas plants because they want power right now, not because clean power can't do the job if it's planned for.

pushback.if: But look at all the new gas plants being built for data centres.
pushback.reply: That part is a real problem. Tech companies want power immediately, and gas is the quickest thing to plug into today's grid. That is a policy choice rather than a physical need: solar with storage, hydro, geothermal and existing nuclear can all serve the same demand if they get the same lead time.

pushback.if: AI could triple electricity demand.
pushback.reply: Even the most pessimistic public forecasts take data centres to about 6% of global electricity, which is a lot but not a runaway. And "could" is carrying a heavy load in that sentence: over 40 years of computing, efficiency has kept beating the panic scenarios.

pushback.if: Individuals should stop using AI to reduce their footprint.
pushback.reply: That isn't where the leverage is. Next to driving, flying, heating a home or what you eat, personal AI use barely registers. The pressure that changes things is on **tech companies** to source clean power and publish real numbers.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*, Chatto & Windus, 2024. Question 12: "Won't we need more fossil fuels to keep up with artificial intelligence?
International Energy Agency, *Electricity 2024*
J. Koomey, Koomey's Law of computing efficiency

claims.claim: air conditioning is a luxury the climate can't afford
heard_as: AC is destroying the climate
We can't afford air conditioning for everyone
AC use should be rationed
It's a lifestyle issue
The West should give up AC first
People survived without AC before
AC drives the climate crisis
claims.kernel: Air conditioning does use a lot of electricity, and it does strain the grid on the hottest days. Its emissions are real. It's also easy to see it as a rich-country habit, since the places with the most AC per person are wealthy ones like the US. If you picture the US electricity draw on a July afternoon and imagine India reaching the same level, "AC is a luxury we can't afford" sounds sensible.
claims.truth: There are around **2 billion AC units** in the world today, and that is expected to reach 6 billion by 2050, roughly a tripling. AC already accounts for 3-4% of world greenhouse gas emissions and about 8% of world electricity. Most of the growth comes from rising incomes in low- and middle-income countries, where people who could not afford cooling finally can. Heating still causes about 4× more global emissions than cooling. So the idea that cooling is driving the climate crisis gets the ratio the wrong way round. Efficient units cut demand nearly in half: - With today's typical inefficient units, global cooling electricity demand reaches 6,200 TWh by 2050, up from 2,000 TWh in 2020. - With efficient units that already exist, demand only reaches 3,400 TWh. - The difference is about the size of the entire EU's electricity use. Inefficient units dominate because of cost. Poor households buying their first AC often can't find the extra $100 for the efficient model, and that gap locks them into years of higher bills. A family buying a 50% more efficient unit could save around $2,000 over the following years. Grid strain is real, but efficiency makes it manageable: - **US**: cooling is already about 30% of peak electricity demand on hot days. With efficient units, that could fall to just over 20% by 2050. - **India**: cooling is about 10% of peak today. With inefficient units it could rise to about 45% by 2050, a huge strain on the grid. With efficient units, it would be only about 20%. Solar helps too. Cooling demand peaks when the sun is shining, so a grid with lots of solar can meet it without a big rise in emissions.
claims.say_this: In a warming world, cooling is a necessity: it saves lives, lets people sleep and work, and helps children learn. The thing to fix is efficiency, because switching to the efficient units we already have would cut cooling electricity nearly in half, and heating still causes four times more emissions than cooling anyway.

pushback.if: AC is causing the climate to warm even more.
pushback.reply: It adds some, yes, but heating emits 4× more, so if emissions are the worry, start with heating. If grid strain is the worry, the answer is efficient units rather than banning AC.

pushback.if: But people in Asia getting AC will double emissions.
pushback.reply: Only if they buy inefficient units and the electricity comes from coal. Efficient units on solar-heavy grids cut cooling emissions to a small fraction of the simple projection, which makes efficient AC one of the cheapest emissions cuts on offer.

pushback.if: Rich people don't need it, they should just adapt.
pushback.reply: Rich people already have it. The people who most need it, for basic health and to be able to work, are lower-income households in tropical countries where heat is now dangerous. Calling cooling a luxury means telling them to sweat it out, and that isn't a workable climate policy.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*, Chatto & Windus, 2024
IEA, The Future of Cooling, 2018, and follow-up reports

claims.claim: we can just keep burning fossil fuels and capture the CO2
heard_as: Carbon capture will fix it
We can just capture the CO2
Why cut fossil fuels when we can just clean up the CO2?
CCS is the answer
Direct air capture will save us
We can suck the carbon out of the sky later
Net zero doesn't mean zero, it means capture the rest
claims.kernel: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) does work in the right conditions, and the idea is appealing. Keep the power stations and factories we already have, fit a unit to the chimney, pump the CO2 underground, and carry on. It also comes up in serious places: oil company plans, IPCC reports, government net-zero strategies. So it's natural to assume it is doing more than it actually is.
claims.truth: CCS captures a very small share of global emissions, and its track record is poor. - CCS runs at **45 sites** worldwide, capturing about 50 million tonnes of CO2 a year. That is around 0.1% of global emissions (Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*). - Around 50 more plants could be running by 2030, taking the total to about 0.4% of emissions. - Even a very optimistic scenario, capturing 1 billion tonnes a year by 2030 (a figure that appears in many net-zero plans), would cover only 2% of world emissions. - By 2020, 149 CCS projects were supposed to be running. More than 100 were cancelled. - In the US, around 80% of CCS projects have failed, mostly because of cost or immature technology. Where CCS can help is a short list: the last 20 to 30% of electricity in regions with little sun and wind, and industries that are hard to clean up, such as **cement, steel and fertiliser**, which together make up about 15% of world emissions. For transport and most electricity it has no real role, because solar, wind and batteries do the job more cheaply. Cost matters too. Oxford researchers compared two paths: one where CCS delivers half of all emission cuts, and one where it delivers a tenth. The CCS-heavy path costs over $1 trillion more per year, adding up to tens of trillions by 2050.
claims.say_this: Carbon capture is real and it has a role, but it can't let us carry on burning fossil fuels. All the capture plants in the world today catch about a thousandth of global emissions, and even the most hopeful plans for 2030 only reach about 2%. We still need to cut fossil fuels fast and keep carbon capture for the few places where nothing cheaper works, like cement and steel.

pushback.if: So we should invest heavily in CCS then?
pushback.reply: Some investment makes sense so the technology keeps improving, but far less than goes to solar, wind, batteries and electrification. Relying on CCS everywhere costs much more than using it only where nothing else works.

pushback.if: Isn't it in every credible net-zero plan?
pushback.reply: Yes, as a small backstop for the hard cases (cement, steel, fertiliser), not as a replacement for cutting fossil fuel use. When an oil company makes CCS its main strategy, that is a different claim from the one climate scientists are making.

pushback.if: Fossil fuel companies can afford it, so why not make them pay?
pushback.reply: They can, and they should. In 2022 they made about $4 trillion in profit. At roughly $100 a tonne, that could have paid to capture 40 billion tonnes, more than a year of global emissions. Money isn't the obstacle, political will is. And even then, capture would do nothing about the other harms of extracting fossil fuels: air pollution, methane leaks, spills and land use.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, University of Oxford. Cost modelling of CCS-heavy and CCS-light pathways
IEA, Global CCUS status

claims.claim: China emits more than us, so why should we bother
heard_as: we're only 1% of global emissions
China opens a coal plant every week
nothing we do matters while they keep building
claims.kernel: China is the largest annual emitter, at roughly **30% of global CO2**, and it is still building coal plants. Those facts are correct, and brushing them aside costs you credibility straight away.
claims.truth: Per person, Chinese emissions are well below American ones. Historically, the US and Europe put up most of the CO2 already in the atmosphere, and it stays there for centuries, so much of the warming we have now comes from us. China also installs more solar and wind than the rest of the world combined, and it dominates the manufacture of the panels, batteries and EVs everyone else is buying. The idea that China is doing nothing has been out of date for years.
claims.say_this: China emits the most in total, but about half as much per person as the US. It also installs more solar and wind than the rest of the world put together, so it isn't the one standing still.

pushback.if: They're still building coal plants
pushback.reply: They are, and it is a real problem. They are also building more clean power than everyone else combined. Both are true at once.

pushback.if: But we're tiny, it makes no difference
pushback.reply: All the countries under 2% each add up to about a third of global emissions. If being small means you're exempt, a third of the problem is exempt.

sources.label: Our World in Data, CO2 emissions.

claims.claim: clean energy relies on child labour and exploitation
heard_as: EVs run on child labour
Green energy = blood diamonds
You're powering your Tesla with cobalt from Congo mines
Renewables aren't ethical
Clean tech has a dirty secret
Electric cars exploit African workers
claims.kernel: The reporting on cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is horrifying, and it is accurate. Children do work in small informal mines. People do die in mine collapses, and toxic exposure damages workers' health. Anyone who reads about it is right to be angry, and right to wonder whether the EV on their driveway is part of it. Where the argument slips is in applying that concern only to clean tech, while ignoring the same cobalt in the phone in your pocket and the cobalt once used in petrol car catalytic converters.
claims.truth: Cobalt has been called the "blood diamond of batteries". - **74% of world cobalt** is mined in the DRC. - Informal mining there is often brutally exploitative: hundreds of thousands of workers, including children, are paid a few dollars a day. - Mine collapses, falling rocks, chemical exposure and eye damage are common. - EVs are now the biggest single use of cobalt, at 45%. Electronics such as phones and laptops use 26%. The DRC itself is very poor: - More than 60% of people live on less than $2 a day. - 80% don't have electricity or safe drinking water. - Mining is 90% of the country's exports and a vital income for millions. Other minerals carry similar risks: - About 50% of world mineral reserves are in countries with "weak" or "poor" governance scores. - That includes 94% of rare earths, 70% of cobalt, 59% of nickel, 41% of copper and 34% of lithium. There are signs of change: - BloombergNEF's cobalt forecasts keep falling. In 2019 it predicted over 300,000 tonnes of cobalt would be needed by 2030. Three years later, that forecast was under 150,000 tonnes. - Tesla now puts LFP batteries, which contain no cobalt, in more than half its new cars. - BYD is investing in sodium-ion batteries, which use neither cobalt nor lithium. - The EU Critical Raw Materials Act (2023) requires regular supply chain audits and caps how much of a mineral can come from a single country.
claims.say_this: The abuse in cobalt mines in Congo is real and urgent, but the same cobalt goes into your phone and laptop, and clean energy is one of the few industries actually moving away from it. It's a problem to fix in the supply chain, not a reason to keep burning coal.

pushback.if: So EVs are built on child labour.
pushback.reply: Some of them, partly, yes. So is the phone in your pocket, and so is fossil fuel refining (cobalt is used as a catalyst in petrol engines). This is a problem across global supply chains, and clean energy is one of the sectors moving away from cobalt fastest.

pushback.if: We should boycott these countries.
pushback.reply: It sounds simple, but it would backfire. Mining is a huge share of DRC income and one of the main ways people make a living there, so cutting the country out would push millions further into poverty without ending the exploitation. What helps is reforming supply chains: better wages, safer conditions and getting children into school.

pushback.if: Switching to LFP batteries fixes everything.
pushback.reply: It removes cobalt from that battery, which is a real win. LFP still uses lithium, though, which has its own mining and water concerns. Sodium-ion batteries use neither cobalt nor lithium, and each generation of the technology has fewer contested materials, so things are improving.

pushback.if: Rich countries just import the problem.
pushback.reply: That's also true. The rich countries buying phones and EVs know what is happening in the DRC and don't do enough about it. Mining countries and importing countries share the responsibility, and conditions will only improve with pressure from both ends of the chain.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*, Chatto & Windus, 2024
Amnesty International, DRC cobalt reports
European Union, Critical Raw Materials Act, 2023
BloombergNEF, cobalt demand forecasts

claims.claim: clean energy uses too much water to be sustainable
heard_as: EVs use tons of water to make
Lithium mining is draining Chile
Solar panels use lots of water
Green energy is destroying water supplies
Renewables aren't sustainable because of water
It's a water disaster
claims.kernel: The local water impacts are real and severe. In parts of northern Chile, mining uses more than half of all the fresh water in the region, and Indigenous communities have been badly affected. Investigative reporting on lithium and copper mining focuses on exactly these places. If you've read it, "mining is killing water supplies" is a documented fact in those areas. Where it goes wrong is in stretching that into "clean energy uses too much water" worldwide, when the fossil fuel system uses far more.
claims.truth: Where the local problem is real: - **16% of critical mineral mines** are in areas with high water stress, meaning demand comes close to or exceeds the water available. - For copper and lithium, about half of world supply comes from regions with high or extreme water stress. - In parts of northern Chile, mining uses over half of all fresh water, causing serious conflict with local communities. But mining is a small share of overall water use. Even in Chile, mining uses just 4% of water, while farming uses 72%. Today, EVs use more water than petrol cars: - In China, an EV uses 262 m³ of water over its life, against 137 m³ for a petrol car, almost double. - In the US, an EV uses about ⅓ more water than a petrol car. - The reason is that 82% of that water goes into making the electricity, not building the car or battery, and most electricity is still made from fossil fuels. Once the electricity is clean, EVs win on water too. Charged with solar or wind, they use about two-thirds less water than petrol cars. Compared with fossil power: - Solar and wind use 5-10× less water than natural gas per unit of electricity. - Solar and wind use 10-100× less water than coal. - Coal, gas and nuclear plants all need huge volumes of water to cool their equipment. Solar panels and wind turbines need almost none. Water use for power in the US is already falling as the country moves from coal to gas and then to solar and wind.
claims.say_this: Overall, clean energy uses far less water than fossil fuels, because coal, gas and nuclear plants need huge amounts for cooling and solar and wind don't. The real problem is local: lithium and copper mining in a few dry places like northern Chile, and that needs fixing there.

pushback.if: But EVs use more water than petrol cars.
pushback.reply: Today, yes, because the electricity is mostly from fossil fuels, and those power plants need enormous amounts of cooling water. As the grid gets cleaner, EVs cross over to using less water than petrol cars, and on a solar and wind grid they use two-thirds less.

pushback.if: Chile is running out of water because of lithium.
pushback.reply: Northern Chile has a real crisis, and lithium brine extraction is part of it. The fix is **direct lithium extraction** (DLE), which pulls lithium from brine without evaporating the water, and it is already being used. Still, lithium mining uses 4% of water in Chile and farming uses 72%, so both need tackling.

pushback.if: So clean energy is fine on water then?
pushback.reply: Locally, no: some mining regions are being pushed to their water limits. Globally, yes: clean energy uses far less water than the fossil system it replaces. Both are true.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*, Chatto & Windus, 2024
WRI Aqueduct, Water Stress Atlas
IEA, water use per unit of energy

claims.claim: Wind turbine blades and solar panels just end up in landfill
heard_as: they're burying blades in the desert
nobody can recycle solar panels
the waste from clean tech will be the next crisis
claims.kernel: There are real photographs of buried turbine blades. A wave of equipment installed over the last two decades is now reaching the end of its life. The problem is not imaginary.
claims.truth: It is a real problem of a modest size. Solar panel waste could add up to **160 million tonnes by 2050**. By the same date, total e-waste is projected at around 1.8 billion tonnes and plastic waste at over 12 billion tonnes, so solar is a rounding error next to waste streams nobody campaigns about. Recycling is also growing fast, especially for batteries. China's GEM recovers over 90% of the lithium from used batteries and processed around 17,000 tonnes of EV batteries in 2022. Redwood Materials found that many packs it takes in still hold more than half their capacity, so it is turning them into solar-powered microgrids instead of shredding them.
claims.say_this: By 2050 the world will have about 160 million tonnes of old solar panels to deal with, against more than 12 billion tonnes of plastic waste. It's a real problem, but a small one, and recycling is already catching up.

pushback.if: Recycling never actually happens
pushback.reply: For plastic, that's largely fair. For batteries it is already a real industry, because the materials inside are valuable enough to be worth recovering.

sources.label: MIT Technology Review, GEM battery recycling, 4 October 2023.
Inside Climate News, solar panel waste reality check, 12 October 2023.

claims.claim: The climate has always changed
heard_as: there were ice ages before humans
it was warmer in medieval times
it's just natural cycles
claims.kernel: It's completely true. The climate has changed many times, sometimes dramatically, long before anyone was burning anything.
claims.truth: Every one of those past changes had a cause we can name: orbital cycles, volcanic activity, shifts in the sun's output, changes in ocean circulation. We measure all of these today, and none of them accounts for the current warming. The rise does closely track the CO2 from burning fossil fuels. Speed is the other difference. Past natural shifts unfolded over many thousands of years, which gave ecosystems time to move. This one is happening over **about 150 years**, far faster than anything in the records we have.
claims.say_this: It has, and each time we can name what caused it. We measure all of those causes today, and none of them explains the warming we're seeing now.

pushback.if: Scientists said there was a pause in warming
pushback.reply: There was a slower decade, then a surge. Ocean heat kept rising the whole time, and that's where over 90% of the extra heat goes.

sources.label: United Nations, Climate Mythbusters.
World Resources Institute (WRI), ocean warming, 2026.

claims.claim: the energy transition will destroy jobs
heard_as: Green jobs won't replace real jobs
The transition will hollow out coal towns
Oil workers will be thrown on the scrap heap
You can't retrain a coal miner as a solar installer
Clean energy pays less than fossil fuels
Climate policy is a war on workers
claims.kernel: In particular places and industries, the transition will hurt real people. Coal towns, oil towns and engineering communities built around a refinery do face job losses, and pretending otherwise would be wrong. Anyone living in one of those places who reads about a coal plant closing has good reason to worry. Where it goes wrong is in stretching that local pain into "the whole transition destroys jobs."
claims.truth: Total energy jobs are rising: - They went from 63 million in 2019 to 68 million in 2023. - They could reach 72 million by 2030, or 82 million on a stronger climate pathway. - **Clean energy jobs overtook fossil fuel jobs in 2021**, because far more money now flows into clean energy. The same is happening in rich countries: - US energy jobs grew 3.8% in 2022, faster than the economy as a whole. Clean energy jobs grew 3.9%. - UK "green jobs" are growing at 4× the normal market rate. Most clean energy jobs can't be sent abroad. Installing solar panels, fitting heat pumps, building EV charging points and insulating homes all have to happen locally, which makes these jobs harder to lose to politics or trade. Hannah Ritchie's figures on the jobs at risk: - About 6 million workers could lose jobs in the traditional petrol and diesel car industry by 2030. Roughly two thirds of them could move to related EV or parts jobs with retraining. VW has pledged to train 22,000 people, Mercedes has invested more than €1.3bn, and Ford US has put in more than $11bn. - About 2.5 million could lose oil and gas jobs. About three quarters of them could move into other parts of the energy industry, with proper investment in retraining. - 32 million people worldwide work in fossil fuels, about 0.4% of the world's population. Climate change affects the other 99.6%.
claims.say_this: Fossil fuel jobs are shrinking, but clean energy jobs are growing faster, and total energy jobs rose from 63 million in 2019 to 68 million in 2023. The real task is looking after the workers whose jobs go, with retraining, support and a frank conversation about pay.

pushback.if: But real people in real towns are going to lose their livelihoods.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that is why a **just transition**, one that looks after affected workers, can't be optional. The UK's last coal power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar (closed 2023), shows how: most of its several hundred workers moved to other jobs at the company or retrained with partners, with only a handful of forced job losses. It worked because planning started years before closure, not months.

pushback.if: Wind turbine installers don't earn what oil workers earn.
pushback.reply: That's true, and it should be said plainly. A wind installer usually earns less than an offshore oil worker, so some people will move into cleaner jobs at lower pay. The fix is to pay clean energy jobs properly and top up wages during the transition where needed.

pushback.if: Governments will leave workers stranded when the plant closes.
pushback.reply: They will if they wait until closure is a few months away. Ratcliffe shows what works: plan years ahead, involve the workforce and fund retraining directly. Where the political will exists, this is a solved policy problem.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*, Chatto & Windus, 2024
IEA, World Energy Employment, 2023

claims.claim: The battery dies after a few years and costs a fortune to replace
heard_as: battery lifetime is horribly uncertain
you'll need a new battery at 8 years
the replacement costs more than the car is worth
claims.kernel: Almost everyone has had a phone whose battery died within two years, so it's a reasonable thing to assume. EV battery packs are managed and cooled very differently, though.
claims.truth: An analysis of 15,000 EVs by Recurrent Motors found that only **1.5% had needed a battery replacement**. Of the cars past 100,000 miles, 90% still held at least 90% of their original range. Most manufacturers guarantee the battery pack for at least eight years. Nissan UK reported that almost all of the batteries it has ever made are still in cars, after twelve years of selling them.
claims.say_this: In a study of 15,000 EVs, only 1.5% had needed a new battery. Most cars past 100,000 miles still had 90% of their range.

pushback.if: And then it goes to landfill
pushback.reply: It doesn't. Packs with half their capacity left are being reused as grid storage, and recyclers recover over 90% of the lithium.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, Factcheck: 21 misleading myths about electric vehicles.

claims.claim: An EV has to drive 50,000 miles before it beats a petrol car
heard_as: the battery emissions cancel out the savings
you'd have to drive it for decades to break even
the e-Golf takes 77,000 miles to pay off
the Volvo C40 needs 68,400 miles
claims.kernel: Building a battery does create more emissions up front, so an EV starts life with a carbon debt. That part is true, and it's where the big number comes from.
claims.truth: The debt is paid back far faster than the widely quoted figures suggest. Carbon Brief puts the break-even point at **roughly 11,000 to 13,000 miles** in Europe and the UK, which is under two years of average driving. The very high numbers came from manufacturers' own studies. These overestimated battery emissions, underestimated the emissions from producing petrol, and used lab fuel economy instead of real-world figures. When independent researchers corrected them, the VW e-Golf broke even at about 14,000 miles rather than 77,000, and the Volvo C40 at about 16,000 rather than 68,400.
claims.say_this: The battery does start with a carbon debt, but it pays it off in about a year and a half of normal driving. Everything after that is a gain.

pushback.if: But I read it was 70,000 miles
pushback.reply: Those figures came from the carmakers' own studies. Independent researchers rechecked the same cars and got about 15,000 miles.

pushback.if: That is only because you assume clean electricity
pushback.reply: No, those figures use European grid averages as they are today. And the grid keeps getting cleaner, while a petrol car never does.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, Factcheck: 21 misleading myths about electric vehicles.

claims.claim: EVs just move the pollution to the power station
heard_as: the electricity has to come from somewhere
they run on coal
long tailpipe
claims.kernel: The electricity does have to come from somewhere, and on a coal-heavy grid an EV is dirtier than it would be on a clean one. The real question is whether it still beats burning petrol, and it does.
claims.truth: An electric motor is roughly four times more efficient than a combustion engine, so an EV wins even where the grid is dirty. Over its whole life, an EV's emissions are about two fifths lower in coal-heavy Poland and two thirds lower in the UK. In China, where coal supplied 61% of power in 2022, an EV still breaks even after about 22,000 miles. The 2021 ICCT global study found cuts of **60 to 70% in the US and Europe**, 35 to 45% in China and 20 to 35% in India. An EV also keeps improving as the grid gets cleaner, while a petrol car is as clean on day one as it will ever be.
claims.say_this: Even on Poland's coal-heavy grid an EV cuts emissions by about 40%, because the motor is four times more efficient. And it gets cleaner every year, which a petrol car never does.

pushback.if: Not where I live, our grid is fossil heavy
pushback.reply: Fair enough, the saving is smaller there. It's still a saving, and it grows every year without you doing anything.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, Factcheck: 21 misleading myths about electric vehicles.
ICCT, A global comparison of the life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions of combustion engine and electric passenger cars, 2021.

claims.claim: Electric cars catch fire and explode
heard_as: they burn down car parks
that ship fire was caused by an EV
you can't put the fire out
claims.kernel: Battery fires behave differently and are harder for firefighters to put out, so the concern isn't made up. They are also very newsworthy, which is exactly why they feel common.
claims.truth: Norwegian data for 2018 to 2022 records about **30 fires per 100,000** conventional cars a year, against about 5 per 100,000 EVs. That means petrol and diesel cars catch fire five to six times more often. The Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency puts the gap at twenty times. The EU-funded LASH FIRE programme concluded that EVs are no more hazardous than conventional cars. The Fremantle Highway cargo ship fire in July 2023 was widely blamed on an EV, but the investigation found the cause was unrelated. In August 2023, the International Union of Marine Insurers stated that no fire on a car carrier had ever been proven to start in a factory-new EV.
claims.say_this: EV fires make the news because they're rare. Per vehicle, petrol and diesel cars catch fire five to six times more often.

pushback.if: But when they do burn you can't stop it
pushback.reply: True, they are harder to put out. That calls for the right firefighting equipment, but it doesn't mean they burn more often.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, Factcheck: 21 misleading myths about electric vehicles.

claims.claim: Hydrogen or synthetic fuel is the real answer, not batteries
heard_as: hydrogen cars are more sustainable
e-fuels will save the combustion engine
we should wait for the better technology
claims.kernel: Both technologies are real and both matter, just not for cars. Hydrogen has a serious role in steel, shipping and long-haul freight, and e-fuels will probably be needed for aviation. So it's reasonable to wonder why they shouldn't power cars too.
claims.truth: For passenger cars the energy maths is unforgiving. UK government lifecycle analysis finds hydrogen cars use about three times more energy than EVs, with 60 to 70% higher emissions, even assuming low-carbon hydrogen. The market has already made its choice: at the end of 2022 there were 72,000 hydrogen vehicles worldwide against 26 million EVs, a ratio of about **360 to 1**. E-fuels cost up to three times more than conventional fuel, need roughly five times more electricity than running an EV, and have lifecycle emissions 53% higher. The IPCC expects the limited supply to go to aviation and shipping.
claims.say_this: Hydrogen and e-fuels matter for planes, ships and steel. For cars they need three to five times more electricity to go the same distance, which is why there are 26 million EVs and only 72,000 hydrogen cars.

pushback.if: The technology will improve
pushback.reply: Some, but the losses come from physics, not engineering. Turning electricity into a fuel and back into motion will always waste more than using the electricity directly.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.

claims.claim: The grid can't cope and there aren't enough chargers anyway
heard_as: we'd need 20 new nuclear power stations
the charging network is at crisis point
the lights will go out if everyone plugs in
claims.kernel: Anyone who has queued at a motorway charger knows public charging can be poor. That frustration is real, even if the numbers behind the bigger claim are not.
claims.truth: National Grid itself lists the grid claim as a myth. The 2017 story that Britain would need 20 new nuclear plants was a miscalculation and was later corrected. Most charging happens at home overnight, off peak, when there is spare capacity on the network. Chargers are growing fast too. UK public charge points passed 50,000 in October 2023, up 43% in a year, against a government target of 300,000 by 2030. The IEA found charging infrastructure kept pace with EV growth in 2022, with a 55% increase. Meanwhile UK EV sales grew 36% year on year over the first nine months of 2023, which is not what a crisis looks like.
claims.say_this: Most charging happens at home overnight, when the grid has spare capacity. National Grid even lists this one as a myth on its own website.

pushback.if: I don't have a driveway
pushback.reply: That is the real gap in this argument, and it's worth pressing your council on. It's a problem of rollout, and rollout can be fixed. The grid itself can cope.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.

claims.claim: Keeping my old car running is greener than buying a new EV
heard_as: old bangers are the green choice
the greenest car is the one you already own
manufacturing a new car is worse than running an old one
it can't be worth scrapping a car that's only a year or two old
claims.kernel: You avoid the emissions of building a whole new car, and "use what you already have" is usually sound environmental advice. It's a sensible instinct.
claims.truth: That instinct holds for most products, but cars are different because they keep emitting every day you drive them. A 14 year old petrol car produces around **45 tonnes of CO2** over its remaining life, against 14 tonnes for a new Tesla Model Y, a cut of about 68%. Even counting the emissions of building the new car, swapping an old petrol car for an EV breaks even after roughly 20,000 to 32,000 miles, about four years of average UK driving.
claims.say_this: For a fridge or a phone, keeping the old one usually wins. For a car it doesn't, because most of the damage comes from the fuel, not the factory.

pushback.if: So I should scrap a perfectly good car?
pushback.reply: Not scrap it. It gets resold and someone else drives it. The real question is what you buy when your old car is truly done, and at that point the EV wins clearly.

pushback.if: Surely that's only true for an old banger, not a car I just bought?
pushback.reply: US modelling from 2026 (Campbell & Geyer, UC Santa Cruz / UC Santa Barbara) tested exactly that. It found the same result holds "in the vast majority of cases, and even for a brand new gas vehicle": the driving emissions saved by switching outweigh the extra emissions of building the new EV. The main exceptions are a coal-heavy electricity grid, or driving under about 7,000km a year.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.
New Scientist, Madeleine Cuff, 6 August 2026.

claims.claim: Electric cars alone won't solve climate change
heard_as: swapping every car for an electric one isn't the answer
it's just consumerism with a green badge
we need to drive less, not drive electric
claims.kernel: It's true as stated, and it's a fair warning against imagining we can swap every car one for one and carry on exactly as before. Someone saying this is often closer to your view than they sound.
claims.truth: It only becomes a problem when it's used as a reason to do nothing. The IPCC judges EVs likely to be essential for cutting transport emissions. It finds that new technology could deliver about **50%** of land transport emissions cuts by 2050, within a range of 30 to 70%. Changes to infrastructure contribute around 30% and changes in behaviour around 5%. So EVs are roughly half the answer, and fewer cars, smaller cars and better public transport make up the rest. We need both.
claims.say_this: I completely agree, they're about half the answer for transport. The other half is fewer and smaller cars and better public transport. It was never one or the other.

pushback.if: So why push EVs at all?
pushback.reply: Because half is a lot, and because most people are not giving up their car this decade. We can do the easier half while we work on the harder half.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.
WRI, smaller EVs.

claims.claim: EVs will soon cost more to run than petrol cars
heard_as: electricity prices will catch up
public charging is more expensive than petrol
wait until they tax the electricity
claims.kernel: There is a real point buried here. If you rely entirely on public rapid chargers, the cost per mile can get close to petrol, and that is where these stories come from.
claims.truth: Carbon Brief's comparison found EV drivers save on fuel in every country it looked at, from the UK and Norway to the US, China, India, Argentina and Australia. Charging at home on an off-peak tariff costs much less than public fast charging, and most drivers charge at home overnight. The UK Climate Change Committee concluded that EVs will be significantly cheaper than petrol and diesel cars to own and run over their lifetimes, once both servicing and fuel are counted.
claims.say_this: If you charge at home overnight, it isn't close: the EV is much cheaper. Public rapid charging is where the gap narrows, and most people rarely use it.

pushback.if: They will tax it eventually
pushback.reply: Probably, since the money from fuel duty has to be replaced somehow. That's a question of tax policy, and it doesn't change the underlying energy cost, which stays lower for EVs.

sources.label: Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.

claims.claim: Heavy EVs produce more pollution from tyres and brakes than petrol cars
heard_as: tyre particulates are worse than exhaust
your super heavy EV pollutes more
non-exhaust emissions
claims.kernel: Heavier vehicles do wear their tyres faster, and dust from tyres and roads is a real air quality problem that gets far less attention than exhaust fumes. This one has a solid core.
claims.truth: The comparison is usually lopsided, though. A petrol car also wears its tyres and brakes, and has an exhaust pipe on top. EVs use **regenerative braking**, where the motor does most of the slowing down, which cuts brake dust a lot. Where the argument does have force is on size, whatever the engine. A Hummer EV is responsible for about 341 grams of CO2 per mile, more than a petrol Toyota Corolla at 269 grams, according to a 2022 Quartz analysis. The fair version of this point is an argument against enormous cars, and it applies to petrol ones as much as electric ones.
claims.say_this: Tyre dust is a real problem, but a petrol car has tyres and brakes too, plus an exhaust. If the worry is heavy vehicles, the target should be huge cars, whatever powers them.

pushback.if: So you admit big EVs are bad
pushback.reply: Yes, a two and a half tonne electric SUV is a poor answer. So is a two and a half tonne petrol one. Smaller cars win either way.

sources.label: MIT Technology Review, huge EVs.
Carbon Brief, 21 EV myths factchecked.

claims.claim: electric cars catch fire all the time
heard_as: EVs spontaneously combust
Lithium batteries are ticking time bombs
You can't park an EV in an underground garage
One EV fire could take down a whole car park
Fire brigades can't put EV fires out
Electric cars are a fire hazard
claims.kernel: EV fires get dramatic news coverage. A lithium-ion battery fire burns hot, is hard to put out, and makes for vivid video. A single EV fire tends to get coverage that a petrol car fire never would. Repeat that a few times and people start to believe EVs are always catching fire. When a big fire in a London airport car park in 2024 was reported as an EV fire, that stuck, even after it turned out to have started in a **diesel Range Rover**.
claims.truth: Data from several sources says EVs catch fire less often than petrol cars: - **Global data 2010-2020**: about 0.004% of EVs and plug-in hybrids caught fire, against 0.08% of petrol cars. That makes the petrol rate **19 times higher**. - **Norway** (which has more EVs per person than anywhere else): fewer fires per 100,000 EVs than for petrol, diesel or other cars, every year from 2018 to 2022. That's about 4 fires per 100,000 EVs on the road, which is very rare. - **EV FireSafe**, an Australian group backed by the Department of Defence, puts the risk that a given EV catches fire at 0.0012%.
claims.say_this: EVs actually catch fire much less often than petrol cars, about 19 times less often going by global data. What's true is that when they do burn, they're harder to put out, so the answer is better batteries and better training for fire crews, not going back to petrol.

pushback.if: But when they burn, they burn hotter and longer.
pushback.reply: That's right, and it's the real safety issue. If a lithium-ion battery short-circuits in a crash, it can go into **thermal runaway**: a reaction that feeds itself and is hard to stop. These fires burn hotter than petrol fires and take much longer to put out, so fire crews need different techniques and training.

pushback.if: So they're more dangerous when they do happen.
pushback.reply: More difficult to fight, yes. More likely to happen, no: much less likely. Those are two different things. A rare fire that's hard to put out can still cause less harm overall than a common fire that's easy to put out.

pushback.if: The EV fleet is newer, so the comparison isn't fair.
pushback.reply: Partly true. EVs on the road are younger on average than petrol cars, and older cars catch fire more often through wear and tear. That may explain some of the gap. But even allowing for age, EVs still have a lower fire rate.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
EV FireSafe. Australian government-backed EV fire research
Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection. Vehicle fire statistics 2018-2022

claims.claim: electric cars don't work in cold weather
heard_as: EVs die in the cold
Batteries don't work in winter
You can't drive an EV in Canada
The range collapses when it's freezing
EVs are only for warm climates
Norwegian winters kill EVs
claims.kernel: Because the range drop is real. Compare summer and winter figures for the same car and the winter one is lower. Anyone who has driven an EV through a proper winter can tell you so. This myth doesn't come from nowhere, and the fair answer is "yes, a bit."
claims.truth: The most detailed study comes from the **Norwegian Automobile Federation (NAF)**, which tested 50 different EV models in Norway. Each drove the same route in summer and winter, at temperatures of 0°C to -10°C: - **Average range drop: 19%.** A car with an advertised range of 450 km managed about 364 km in winter. - **Tesla Model Y (best performer): 11% loss** (280 → 226 km) - **Skoda Enyaq iV80 (worst performer): 32% loss** (360 → 245 km) - Similar studies elsewhere find drops of 10 to 20%, so the pattern holds up. - **Fast charging is also slower**: 37 minutes on average in winter against 33 in summer, about 10% slower. Some cars (BMW iX) saw charging time jump by a third. For most drivers this rarely matters. In the US, only about **5% of journeys** are longer than 50 km. Even the EV with the biggest range drop still comfortably handles a 100 km round trip in the cold. The real-world proof: **Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Iceland**, five of the coldest countries in the world, have some of the highest rates of EV ownership anywhere.
claims.say_this: EVs do lose some range in the cold, typically 10 to 20%, and charging is a bit slower. But for everyday driving, well under 100 miles, it barely matters, and the coldest countries, like Norway, Sweden and Finland, have the highest rates of EV ownership.

pushback.if: So EVs lose 20% of their range. That's a lot.
pushback.reply: For an EV with 400 km of range, a 20% drop still leaves 320 km. Very few people drive that far on a normal day. Where it does matter is long winter road trips, and even those are manageable with one extra charging stop.

pushback.if: Nobody wants to be stuck at a charger in the freezing cold.
pushback.reply: That's a fair concern, and there are fixes. Many new EVs have **heat pumps**, which warm the cabin and battery more efficiently. Pre-heating the battery before you reach the charger also brings charging time back closer to summer levels.

pushback.if: What about very extreme cold, like -30°C?
pushback.reply: Range drops further, and public charging gets patchy. The Norwegian tests don't cover Arctic extremes. For driving at -30°C, a hybrid or petrol backup might make more sense, but that's a tiny share of the world's driving.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Norwegian Automobile Federation (NAF). 50-car winter range test

claims.claim: electric cars are just as bad for the climate as petrol cars
heard_as: EVs aren't really green because of the battery
Electric cars have a bigger carbon footprint than petrol cars
The mining and manufacturing cancel out any climate benefit
EVs just move the emissions upstream
Coal-powered EVs are pointless
The lifecycle emissions of an EV are just as bad
claims.kernel: The manufacturing footprint is real and sizeable. Building the battery takes a lot of energy, and much of that energy still comes from fossil fuels today. If you stop counting at the factory gate, an EV really does start out worse than a petrol car. The mistake is stopping there instead of looking at its whole 15-year life on the road.
claims.truth: Once you add up emissions from both making and running the car, EVs come out well ahead everywhere: - **UK**: an EV emits **66% less carbon** than a petrol car over its life. By 2030 this rises to 76% less. - **Europe**: up to 70% lower lifetime emissions - **US**: about two thirds lower - **China** (a grid heavily based on coal): still 37 to 45% lower - **India** (also coal-heavy): nearly a third lower These figures already include the emissions from making the car and its battery. EVs will keep getting cleaner as grids move away from fossil fuels. Manufacturing is improving fast too: **CATL**, the world's largest battery maker, cut its own manufacturing emissions by 45% in a single year by running its factories on more clean electricity.
claims.say_this: Making an electric car does create more carbon upfront than making a petrol one, mostly because of the battery, but you pay that back quickly once you start driving. Over its whole life an EV is 60 to 70% cleaner than a petrol car almost everywhere, and it keeps getting cleaner as the grid does.

pushback.if: But the battery is a huge carbon debt.
pushback.reply: It is, but you pay it back within roughly the first 15,000-30,000 miles, depending on how clean the local electricity is. After that, every mile is far cleaner than in a petrol car. Over 150,000 miles, the battery's debt is small next to the exhaust emissions you avoid.

pushback.if: What about all the mining?
pushback.reply: Mining is a real problem and needs cleaning up. But a petrol car needs mining too, plus **15 years of extracting, refining and burning oil**. So the choice is between mining for a battery once, and mining for a car once and then burning fuel for its whole life.

pushback.if: OK but for someone who barely drives, it's not worth it.
pushback.reply: Fair. If you hardly drive, the climate case for replacing a working petrol car is weak, because the manufacturing emissions take a long time to pay back. For low-mileage drivers the best answer is usually to keep the current car going, then go electric when it needs replacing.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Transport & Environment. Battery electric vehicles lifecycle emissions modelling
IEA. Global EV Outlook 2024

claims.claim: electric cars are only good for short trips
heard_as: You can't take an EV on a road trip
Range anxiety is a real thing
EVs are city cars, not proper cars
You'd never make it to Scotland in one
EVs are only good for the school run
The battery dies too fast
claims.kernel: The myth is about a decade behind the technology. Early EVs really were only good for short trips: the first Nissan Leaf and the BMW ActiveE managed less than 100 miles per charge. That was the best on offer around 2010-2012. People whose picture of EVs dates from then, or who haven't looked closely since, are remembering a very different market accurately.
claims.truth: Range has grown enormously in a decade: - **2010 average EV range: ~80 miles** on a single charge - **2021 average: ~220 miles**, nearly triple - **US average: ~450 miles** (bigger cars are popular there) - Plenty of mainstream models now offer 280+ miles - At the top of the market, the longest-range EV in 2011 (the BMW ActiveE) managed 94 miles. By 2022 the record was **520 miles** (Lucid Air Dream R), and it will keep rising. What people drive each day: - **Average UK driver: 20 miles/day** (even less in a two-car household) - **Average US driver: ~40 miles/day** Both fit easily within the range of even the cheapest new EVs. On long trips, driving on a motorway at the speed limit, you'd cover about 280 miles in 4 hours. Drivers are advised to take a **15-minute break every few hours** anyway, which lines up with when the EV needs a top-up. Battery wear is often exaggerated. Studies across tens of thousands of vehicles find batteries lose about **2% of their capacity per year**, much slower than most people assume.
claims.say_this: That was true in 2010, when the average EV did 80 miles on a charge, but most new EVs now do 200+ miles, plenty do 400+, and the best do over 500. The average UK driver covers 20 miles a day and the average American 40, so range is sorted for daily driving, and the only real gap left is reliable charging on the odd long trip.

pushback.if: But I do a 500-mile road trip once a year.
pushback.reply: You have two options: buy a longer-range EV (they exist), or make one 20-minute charging stop halfway, which you'd take as a break anyway. If it's truly a one-off, some drivers hire a petrol car for that trip. Over 15 years of owning a car, one long trip a year isn't a good reason to choose a worse car for every other day.

pushback.if: What if I can't find a charger?
pushback.reply: That's a real concern, but it's a problem with the **charging network**, and the car itself is fine. If your petrol car ran dry because there were no petrol stations, you'd blame the fuel network, not the car. The fix is more reliable public chargers on the routes people drive.

pushback.if: Batteries degrade over time so range gets worse.
pushback.reply: By about 2% a year, on average. Over 10 years that takes 20% off the starting range, so a 300-mile EV becomes a 240-mile EV. That's still well beyond what almost anyone drives in a day.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA. Global EV Outlook 2024

claims.claim: electric cars pollute just as much as petrol cars
heard_as: EVs still pollute
Tyre particles are just as bad as tailpipe emissions
Electric cars aren't zero-emission
PM2.5 from EVs is worse because they're heavier
You're just moving the pollution around
There's no such thing as a clean car
claims.kernel: "Zero emissions" is a claim EV marketing often makes, and strictly speaking it's wrong. Cars pollute in four ways: exhaust, brake wear, tyre wear and road dust. EVs get rid of only one of them. Anyone pointing out that tyre and road particles still exist is telling the truth. The mistake is treating "not zero" as "the same as petrol."
claims.truth: Every car pollutes the air in four ways: - Exhaust fumes: nitrogen oxides (NOx) and PM2.5 (fine particles small enough to get deep into the lungs). Both are very harmful to breathing, and EVs remove both. - Brake wear: from friction between pads and discs. EVs use **regenerative braking**, so the brakes are used far less often. Much reduced, though not eliminated. - Tyre wear: from friction with the road. About the same, or slightly worse, in EVs because they're heavier. - Road dust: kicked up by moving vehicles, and also affected by weight. Slightly worse in EVs. So EVs cause a little more tyre and road dust pollution, but that is far outweighed by removing exhaust fumes and cutting brake wear. Taking each source in turn, EVs come out cleaner overall. The remaining problem is real, though. **PM2.5 from non-exhaust sources** still harms health, especially in crowded cities.
claims.say_this: EVs still cause some pollution from tyres, brakes and road dust, and because they're heavier they can be a bit worse on tyres and dust. But they get rid of exhaust fumes completely, which is the biggest and most harmful source, so overall they're much better for the air we breathe.

pushback.if: So EVs still cause air pollution.
pushback.reply: Yes, some. But the pollution they remove, NOx and PM2.5 from exhausts, is directly linked to millions of deaths a year worldwide. The pollution they make slightly worse (tyre and road dust) is a smaller problem. Trading one for the other is a big win.

pushback.if: They're heavier because of the battery, so tyre wear is worse.
pushback.reply: True. It's one of the strongest arguments for [smaller EVs](../sectors/transport/smaller-evs-better.md). A smaller EV with a smaller battery is lighter, cheaper, safer for pedestrians and produces less pollution from tyres and road dust. Petrol and electric cars have both got heavier over the past decade, with the "SUV effect" pushing weight up across the board. France has already brought in a weight tax, and that logic should apply to EVs as well as petrol SUVs.

pushback.if: So EVs aren't really clean.
pushback.reply: A fairer way to put it: much cleaner than petrol on the biggest source, slightly worse on the smaller ones. They're not "clean" in an absolute sense. That's why walking, cycling and public transport still beat any car.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
WHO. Ambient air pollution health effects

claims.claim: electric cars are too expensive for the average driver
heard_as: Only rich people can afford electric cars
EVs are a luxury
You need to be rich to go green
The savings only work if you own a house with a driveway
Second-hand EVs are just as expensive as new petrol
Once you factor in the charger install, they're not cheaper
claims.kernel: The price on the showroom windscreen really is higher. If you compare two cars in a dealership today, the EV usually costs more to buy. Most people don't think in terms of "total cost of ownership": they think about monthly payments and the upfront cheque. And for households on tight budgets, that upfront gap is real.
claims.truth: Running costs are already much lower: - **100 miles in an EV costs about £6.** In a petrol car it's £12 to £18, so roughly half or less. - The average UK driver could save up to £1,000 a year, and over **£10,000 across the life of the car**. - A Gulf Oil study across 33 countries found EVs cheaper to run than petrol in almost every country surveyed. - EVs have far fewer moving parts: no oil changes, no exhaust, no catalytic converter, and less brake wear. So maintenance costs less too. Upfront prices are falling: - By **2025**, many mainstream models cost the same in electric and petrol versions. The electric Citroën C4 matched the petrol version's price. - Second-hand EV versions of best-sellers (BMW, Peugeot, Vauxhall, Hyundai, Tesla) are now often **cheaper than the petrol equivalents**. - BYD sells the Seagull in Europe for around **£10,000** with ~250 miles of range, which has pushed VW, Renault and Stellantis to launch EVs under €25,000. But the cost of charging depends on where you do it: - **Home charging: ~£6** per 100 miles - **Public charger: ~£16** per 100 miles - **Rapid charger: ~£18** per 100 miles (similar to petrol)
claims.say_this: A new EV still costs more to buy than a petrol car, but the gap is closing fast, and charging at home costs about half what petrol does. That saves the average UK driver around £1,000 a year and over £10,000 over the car's life, so the real problem is that cheap charging isn't available to everyone yet.

pushback.if: For someone in a flat with no driveway, EVs aren't cheaper.
pushback.reply: That's right, and it's the real unfairness inside the EV story. Someone who can only use rapid public chargers pays roughly what a petrol driver pays. What fixes it is more affordable public and on-street charging.

pushback.if: But I can't afford the upfront £30,000.
pushback.reply: Fair enough, new EVs are still a stretch for many people. **Used EVs** are now often cheaper than used petrol versions of the same model, and that's where most affordable switching will happen over the next few years.

pushback.if: Aren't Chinese EVs being blocked by tariffs?
pushback.reply: Yes, and it's a policy choice that hurts buyers. Some governments have put tariffs on affordable Chinese EVs to protect their own car makers, which makes cars more expensive for ordinary people.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Gulf Oil. 33-country running-cost comparison
BloombergNEF. EV cost parity forecasts

claims.claim: electric cars will break the electricity grid
heard_as: The grid can't handle EVs
We don't have enough electricity for EVs
EVs will cause blackouts
Charging will overload the system
The grid isn't ready
We need to build more power plants for EVs
claims.kernel: If you multiply the numbers naïvely, they look frightening. If every UK driver plugged in at 6:30pm and drew maximum power, peak demand from cars alone would be about **230 GW**, nearly four times the UK's current 60 GW peak. Newspapers love this comparison. It just isn't how charging works.
claims.truth: Real demand from EVs is much smaller, because most cars sit parked most of the time and can charge whenever suits the grid: - There are **33 million cars** in the UK, and the average driver does ~20 miles a day. - Most drivers wouldn't need to charge every day. Once a week is often enough. - National Grid estimates that if all UK cars went electric, peak demand would rise by **25 to 29%**. - If all UK cars, vans and lorries went electric, the peak would rise about 40%. - Total yearly generation would go from ~300 TWh to about 370 TWh (cars only) or 410 TWh (with vans and lorries). - The UK was already generating **400 TWh in 2005**, more than would be needed today even if every car were electric.
claims.say_this: The scary maths only works if every EV charges at exactly the same moment, which never happens: even if every UK car went electric, National Grid estimates peak demand would rise about 25 to 29%, which is manageable. With smart charging, EVs can even help the grid, charging when power is cheap and clean and feeding some back when demand spikes.

pushback.if: But everyone will charge at 6pm when they get home.
pushback.reply: Some will, and that would be a problem, which is why smart charging and off-peak tariffs exist. Pricing that changes with the time of day shifts most charging to overnight (or midday for people with solar panels). Norway already manages this well, spreading charging across morning, evening and overnight.

pushback.if: The grid can't handle a 30% peak rise.
pushback.reply: Grid capacity grows over time as power stations and power lines are added. The UK's peak was **already higher in 2005** than it would be today with every car electric. It fell after 2005 because industry and household appliances became more efficient. EVs will push it back up gradually, in step with grid expansion.

pushback.if: What about extreme weather events, like Texas in winter?
pushback.reply: The Texas grid failed because of a lack of investment, and EVs played no part. But it does point to an opportunity: **vehicle-to-grid (V2G)** turns cars into a backup power source for the grid in exactly that kind of event. Germany and the Netherlands are already piloting V2G.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
UK National Grid. Future Energy Scenarios
IEA. Global EV Outlook 2024

claims.claim: My one flight makes no difference
heard_as: the plane was going anyway
aviation is only 2% of emissions
they'll have clean fuel soon
claims.kernel: Aviation is a small slice of global emissions, so at the global scale the number really is small. The problem with the argument is how unevenly that slice is shared out.
claims.truth: Flying is the quickest way for one person to use up their whole yearly carbon budget, and it's very unequally spread: a small minority of frequent flyers accounts for most aviation emissions. New Scientist reporting found that people on high incomes who care about the environment tend to have larger footprints than their peers, mostly because they fly more. The industry's own plan is off track too. In June 2026 Willie Walsh, head of the airline body IATA, admitted the 2050 net zero pledge will probably not be met, with sustainable aviation fuel at just **0.8%** of its target.
claims.say_this: Flying is the one choice where a single decision really does change your own carbon footprint, because most people on earth never fly at all.

pushback.if: Sustainable fuel will fix it
pushback.reply: The head of the airline industry said in 2026 that its 2050 target probably won't be met. Its green fuel is at under 1% of what was planned.

sources.label: Guardian, IATA net zero admission, June 2026.
New Scientist, wealthy environmentalists.

claims.claim: there's no hope for low-carbon flying and shipping
heard_as: You can't decarbonise flying
Shipping is impossible to fix
Aviation will never be clean
We just have to accept flight emissions
There's no green jet fuel
Long-distance travel is stuck with fossil fuels
claims.kernel: The physics really is unforgiving. A container ship crossing the Pacific carries 80,000 tonnes of cargo for weeks. A jumbo jet lifts hundreds of tonnes to 40,000 feet and burns huge amounts of energy every second to do it. Batteries can't come close to that. Anyone who has read up on replacing jet fuel knows the shortlist is short, and none of the options is easy. So "hopeless" feels grounded, until you look at what is being tested.
claims.truth: Each sector is a fairly small slice of the problem, and both have real options. Some already work for short trips; others are being tested for long ones. How big the problem is: - Aviation: **2-3% of global emissions** - Shipping: 2-3% of global emissions - Aviation's emissions have doubled since 1990 - Aviation adds extra warming from contrails, because water vapour high in the sky warms the planet more than it does at ground level - About 40% of everything shipped around the world is fossil fuels. As we move off fossil fuels, demand for shipping drops by itself. Short trips, already working: - Norway has **60+ electric ferries** running, and short flights are being electrified too - Today's batteries manage about 100 km, which is enough for ferries and short-hop flights but not long-haul Long trips, options being tested: - Biofuels, made from waste fats or vegetable oils. The catch: making all aviation fuel from vegetable oil would need 250-300 million tonnes a year. That is more than double the world's current vegetable oil production, so it would compete with food. - Hydrogen, which is clean where it is used. Powering all of today's aviation with it would need about 4,000 TWh of extra electricity, or 15-20% of the world's electricity today. - Synthetic fuels made from hydrogen. They face similar electricity limits, but existing aircraft can use them without changes. - Direct air capture to offset the emissions. If capturing CO2 from the air gets down to about $100 a tonne, flight fuel costs would rise by about 50%. That is cheaper than hydrogen at today's prices. Commercial progress: - Maersk is building **18 methanol-powered container ships**, expected to be running by the end of 2025 - "Green" methanol costs $320-720 a tonne today. It needs to fall to about $250 to compete with fossil fuel.
claims.say_this: Flying and shipping are the hardest to clean up, but hard isn't impossible: Norway already runs 60+ electric ferries and Maersk is building 18 methanol-powered container ships. They'll probably be the last sectors to get there, not the ones that never do.

pushback.if: Battery-electric long-haul flights are impossible.
pushback.reply: That's right: batteries don't hold enough energy for their weight, and probably won't for decades. But long-haul isn't the only kind of flight. Hydrogen or synthetic fuels can cover it, and batteries work for short-haul, which is a real slice of aviation.

pushback.if: Biofuels compete with food.
pushback.reply: Yes, that is a real limit. Making all aviation fuel from vegetable oil would use more oil than the world grows for food, and fuel from waste fats has a much lower ceiling. So biofuels will probably cover part of aviation, not all of it. That's fine, because no single fuel was ever going to do everything.

pushback.if: Hydrogen aviation needs a fifth of world electricity.
pushback.reply: For all of today's aviation, yes, and that is a real problem of scale. In practice hydrogen flying would grow as the grid grows: the more clean electricity comes online, the more hydrogen makes sense. It doesn't have to solve aviation on day one.

pushback.if: Shipping and aviation avoid climate rules.
pushback.reply: True, and frustrating. No country is responsible for international flights or shipping, so both industries have been able to sidestep climate talks for decades. This is a problem of rules and oversight more than technology. The fix is to bring them formally under UN climate accountability.

claims.claim: Buying local matters more than cutting down on meat
heard_as: food miles are the problem
local beef is fine
it's the transport that does the damage
claims.kernel: Buying local is good for plenty of reasons: it supports local businesses, the food is fresher, you eat with the seasons, and you know how it was produced. Food miles are also easy to picture. The carbon just isn't mostly in the journey.
claims.truth: Transport is a small share of food emissions overall, and almost nothing for the foods with the biggest footprint. For beef, transport is **well under 1%** of the total. Nearly all of it comes from land use and from the methane the animals produce. WRI's analysis finds that, per gram of protein, beef uses around 20 times the land of beans and produces around 20 times the emissions. The 2025 EAT-Lancet report found that a "planetary health" diet would cut agricultural emissions other than CO2 by 15 to 34%, free up an area of land the size of India, and prevent around 15 million deaths a year. Modelling by LSHTM and Cornell, published in Nature, found a healthier global diet could cut land use emissions by 85% by 2050.
claims.say_this: What you eat matters far more than how far it travelled. For beef, transport is under 1% of the footprint.

pushback.if: Irish grass fed beef is different
pushback.reply: It does better than feedlot beef on some measures, but its footprint is still many times that of plants. Eating less beef, and better beef, is the fair answer.

claims.claim: The transition will destroy jobs
heard_as: 40% of US auto jobs will disappear
you're putting whole towns out of work
green jobs don't pay
claims.kernel: There is something real here, though it isn't about the total number of jobs. The jobs lost and the jobs created are rarely in the same towns, for the same people, at the same time. Brushing that aside is how you lose the argument, and it would be fair to lose it.
claims.truth: Overall, clean energy creates more jobs for every pound spent. One study found $1 million of spending supports **7.49 full time jobs** in renewables and 7.72 in energy efficiency, against 2.65 in fossil fuels. So each $1 million moved from fossil fuels to clean energy adds around five jobs. In the US, over $100 billion of announced EV investment is linked to more than 100,000 jobs, and Boston Consulting Group research finds that building an EV takes as much labour as building a petrol or diesel car. FactCheck.org looked into the claim that 40% of US car industry jobs would vanish under EV rules and found no evidence to support it.

pushback.if: Tell that to a refinery town

claims.claim: heat pumps don't work in cold climates
heard_as: Heat pumps don't work when it's freezing
They stop working below zero
You need a gas backup
They can't heat old houses
Nordics only use them because they're rich
They're a scam in cold climates
claims.kernel: It is true that heat pumps lose some efficiency below zero. Every manufacturer publishes performance curves that show it. If you read the spec sheet and stop there, it's natural to conclude "yeah, they must struggle". The mistake is treating a small drop in efficiency as "doesn't work" rather than "still much better than the alternative".
claims.truth: Heat pump efficiency is measured as the **COP (Coefficient of Performance)**: how many units of heat you get for each unit of electricity. A COP of 3 means 1 kWh of electricity gives you 3 kWh of heat. - Between 5°C and –10°C, heat pumps average a COP of about 2.7, which is still very efficient - A field study of 550 heat pumps across Switzerland, Germany, UK, Canada and US found COPs ranging from 3.3 in Canada to 2.5 in China - How that compares: - Gas boiler: 0.7–0.8 (70–80% efficient, because 20–30% of the heat goes up the flue) - Electric radiator: ~1.0 - Heat pump in a UK winter: ~2.7, better than both People who have them agree. Nesta surveyed 2,500 UK heat pump users: - **3 out of 4 people** were happier, or just as happy, with their heat pump compared with their old heating - Satisfaction was similar in old Victorian houses and modern homes, so the "doesn't work in old leaky homes" version of the myth doesn't hold up either The places that use them most: - Norway, Sweden, Finland: the most heat pumps per household in Europe - Alaska: common even where winters drop below –20°C
claims.say_this: They lose a little efficiency in the cold, but they still work: Norway, Sweden and Finland, three of the coldest countries in Europe, have the most heat pumps per household. Even in a UK winter they get about 2.7 units of heat from each unit of electricity, while a gas boiler gets 0.7 to 0.8 from each unit of gas.

pushback.if: But they use loads more electricity when it's cold.
pushback.reply: Yes, that part is true. As the outside temperature falls, so does the COP. On a cold snap in a UK winter a heat pump might run at closer to COP 2.0 or a little below. It still uses less energy than a gas boiler, though it isn't always cheaper to run (see the [cost myth](heat-pumps-too-expensive.md)).

pushback.if: My old Victorian house won't work with one.
pushback.reply: The Nesta survey found similar satisfaction in old and new homes. Good insulation helps any heating system, but a heat pump doesn't need perfect insulation. With radiators of the right size and a competent installer, an old house works fine.

pushback.if: But badly installed ones don't work well.
pushback.reply: This is the real bottleneck. A badly installed heat pump performs poorly. Fitting one is a skilled job that combines engineering, plumbing, pipe-fitting and refrigeration. The UK has roughly **3,000 trained heat pump engineers** and needs closer to 30,000 by 2030. Training is what holds things back, not the technology.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Nesta, UK Heat Pump User Survey (2,500 respondents)
Field study, 550 heat pumps across Switzerland, Germany, UK, Canada, US

claims.claim: heat pumps are too expensive
heard_as: You can't afford a heat pump
They only make sense if you're rich
Even with the grant they're too expensive
Running costs are higher than gas
They're a luxury product
Electricity is too expensive for heat pumps to compete
claims.kernel: The upfront bill really is bigger. In the UK an air-source heat pump costs around £12,000 to install, against £2,750 for a gas boiler. Households don't think in "lifetime cost", they think in "what does the installer's quote say." And even with the grant applied, that quote comes to about £4,500, well above the boiler. That is a real barrier, especially for households on lower incomes, and pretending otherwise doesn't help anyone.
claims.truth: The upfront gap is real, running costs depend on the country, and over a lifetime heat pumps usually come out ahead. Upfront cost in the UK: - Heat pump installation: about **£12,000** (air-source) - Gas boiler: about £2,750 (£2,500-£3,000) - Gap before grants: ~£9,000 - UK government grant: £7,500 - Gap after the grant: ~£2,000 more than a gas boiler That gap falls hardest on people with the least. A Nesta survey found heat pumps are rare in the poorest parts of the UK and common among wealthier households. Even at £2,000 above a boiler, they are out of reach for many. Running cost: - UK electricity costs **~4× more than gas** per unit - A heat pump delivers ~3 units of heat per unit of electricity, so it breaks even at roughly a COP of 3 (the COP, or coefficient of performance, is the units of heat you get per unit of electricity) - The average UK heat pump COP is 2.9, right on the break-even line So in the UK today some households save and some pay more, especially in cold snaps when the COP drops. Elsewhere the picture is better: - Average households in the US, Europe, South Korea and Japan saved money on heating by switching in 2021-22 - Savings in continental Europe grew after gas prices spiked following Russia's invasion of Ukraine Lifetime cost: - Counting installation and running costs over the whole lifespan, heat pumps usually work out **cheaper than a gas boiler**, even in countries where governments pay large subsidies - They typically save a few hundred dollars a year on running costs, which pays back the extra upfront cost over time - They are the cheapest way to take the carbon out of heating, cheaper than direct electric heaters or hydrogen boilers
claims.say_this: Over their lifetime heat pumps usually cost less than a gas boiler, but the upfront price is a real barrier: in the UK it's still about £2,000 more even after the £7,500 grant. That's a problem we can fix with bigger grants and fairer electricity prices, not a problem with the technology.

pushback.if: So they're cheaper only if you can afford the upfront.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that is the real problem hidden inside the wider claim. The direct fix is **bigger grants for lower-income households**. The current UK grant helps middle-income households but isn't enough for those on low incomes.

pushback.if: Electricity is 4× the cost of gas in the UK. There's no way it's cheaper to run.
pushback.reply: The heat pump's efficiency closes most of that gap. At COP 3.0 it uses ⅓ of the energy a boiler does, so 4× the price × ⅓ of the energy ≈ 1.3× the cost, which is close to break-even. Heat pump tariffs from Octopus and OVO can bring running costs below gas: an efficient heat pump on one of these tariffs can halve a household's heating bill.

pushback.if: Energy taxes make electricity more expensive than gas.
pushback.reply: Yes, that's another real part of the problem. In many countries energy taxes sit on electricity rather than gas, mostly because gas was assumed to be what homes used. Moving those taxes off electricity, or onto gas, would tip the sums further towards heat pumps.

UK Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS), £7,500 grant

you need to rip out all your radiators
