claims.truth: A heat pump moves heat rather than making it, so it delivers **roughly three to five units of heat** for every unit of electricity. A gas boiler can never get more than one unit of heat from one unit of gas, because it is limited by the energy in the fuel. As for the cold, the Nordic countries have the highest heat pump adoption in Europe, which answers the physics question fairly directly. Whether it's cheaper to run depends on the local price of electricity compared with gas, and that comes down to taxes and how energy markets are set up rather than the technology.
claims.say_this: A heat pump gives you three to five units of heat for every unit of electricity, because it moves heat instead of burning something. And Norway and Finland, hardly warm places, have the highest adoption in Europe.

pushback.if: My neighbour got one and hated it
pushback.reply: That's most likely a sizing or insulation problem rather than the technology. Bad installation is the single biggest reason owners are unhappy.

heard_as: 100 companies cause 70% of emissions
personal carbon footprints are fossil fuel propaganda
recycling is a distraction
claims.kernel: On the arithmetic, this is right, and history backs it up. BP popularised the personal carbon footprint calculator in 2004, and putting the responsibility on consumers suited the industry very well. Someone making this point is not your opponent.
claims.truth: Individual action was never mainly about the tonnes you save yourself. Its value is that behaviour spreads and what counts as normal shifts: research on social tipping points suggests that once **around 25% of a group** adopts a behaviour, it can be enough to shift the majority. The things that make the biggest difference aren't really individual at all. How you vote, what you say at work, where your pension and bank put your money, and whether you fly all reach well beyond your own footprint. It's also worth knowing that people on high incomes who care about the environment often have bigger footprints than their peers, mostly from flying, so caring on its own doesn't cut emissions.

claims.claim: what happens when the sun doesn't shine and the wind doesn't blow?
heard_as: What about when the sun doesn't shine?
Renewables are intermittent
You need 100% backup
The grid will fail without fossil fuels
Batteries can't store enough
Renewables are only 30% of the time
We can't rely on the weather
claims.kernel: Solar and wind really do come and go. If you assume nothing else about the grid changes, "the lights would go out" is the natural conclusion. Fossil fuel commentators also like the argument, so it gets repeated a lot. What usually gets left out is that grid engineers were dealing with this long before renewables existed: the grid has always had to match demand that changes with supply that changes.
claims.truth: There are three time windows to cover, and each has different answers. **Minutes to hours (the easy part)** - Lithium-ion batteries give back about **98% of the electricity** you put in - They are very efficient and cheap enough for daily use, but not economical for storing power over months - They are already working at grid scale in Australia, California, Texas and elsewhere **Hours to days** - Solar and wind complement each other: solar peaks in the daytime and in summer, while wind is often stronger at night and in winter - Adding hydropower, geothermal and nuclear helps - Sharing across borders: it's always sunny or windy somewhere. Sunny Spain can send power to a cloudy UK, and the UK can return the favour when it's windy. - Modern high-voltage DC cables make this cheap and efficient **Weeks to months (the hard part)** This isn't fully solved yet, but there are three likely answers: - Pumped hydro: water is pumped uphill when power is plentiful and released through turbines later. It gets back ~80% of the energy. It's cheap, but only works where the landscape allows. - Heat storage: electricity is stored as heat in water, rock, sand or molten salt. It's useful for industries that need heat, such as steel, cement and glass. - Hydrogen: electricity makes hydrogen, and hydrogen makes electricity again later. It is only **40-50% efficient** from start to finish, so you lose roughly half the power, but it can be stored at large scale. Chris Goodall worked out the cost of covering two months of UK winter: - With batteries alone: ~£3 trillion per year, more than the UK's entire GDP - With hydrogen: billions to tens of billions per year, expensive but manageable So the job is to match the tool to the timescale: batteries for short gaps, hydrogen or hydro for long ones. Using batteries for months of backup makes no sense.
claims.say_this: Engineers have been planning for this from day one: sun and wind cover for each other most of the time, batteries handle the hours, and sharing power across borders, hydro and nuclear handle the days. Storing power for weeks or months is still being worked out, but hydrogen and heat storage look like the answers.

pushback.if: So it's not solved.
pushback.reply: The short term is solved, and the long term is on its way. Hydrogen and heat storage have been shown to work, they just need building at scale. The gap is no longer "we don't know how". The gap is "we haven't built it at scale yet." Every energy technology starts there.

pushback.if: What if we get a really bad dunkelflaute?
pushback.reply: *Dunkelflaute* is a German word for weeks of little sun and little wind, which is common in northern European winters. It is the specific hard case, and it's why backup from hydrogen, biomass, nuclear or gas with carbon capture makes sense in countries far from the equator. It's a real engineering problem with real solutions, and it affects the last 5-10% of the system, not the whole grid.

pushback.if: You still need gas as backup for renewable systems, so what's the point?
pushback.reply: Keeping some gas for **rare, occasional backup** is far better than running gas plants all the time. If they only run for 100 hours a year in emergencies instead of all 8,760 hours of the year, their emissions fall many times over, even before they are replaced with cleaner sources.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Chris Goodall, UK long-term storage cost analysis

claims.claim: Ireland is too small to make any difference
heard_as: we're 0.1% of global emissions
why should we wreck our economy
let the big countries go first
claims.kernel: Ireland's total emissions really are small, and it's reasonable to ask why a small country should move before the big ones do.
claims.truth: Ireland is small in total but near the top in Europe per person, and the per-person figure is the one that reflects choices rather than population size. Some of those choices are big. Ireland has **107 data centres** operating, drawing about 1.3 GW, and EirGrid, which runs the national grid, forecasts they could take 31% of the country's electricity by 2034. Between 2015 and 2023 the data centres added roughly 360 euro in total to each household's electricity bill. More broadly, all the countries that each emit under 2% add up to roughly a third of global emissions. If being small meant being exempt, a third of the problem would be exempt.
claims.say_this: We're small in total, but near the top in Europe per person. And data centres taking about a third of our electricity by 2034 is nothing small.

pushback.if: We should wait for the big emitters
pushback.reply: All the countries under 2% together make up about a third of global emissions. If they all wait, a third of the problem never moves.

claims.claim: it's too late, we're heading for 5 or 6 degrees, so nothing matters
heard_as: It's too late anyway
We're already screwed
Nothing we do now matters
We're heading for 5 or 6 degrees regardless
The planet is toast
Doomism
Why bother recycling if we're all doomed
The point of no return has passed
We're cooked
claims.kernel: Because part of it is true. The **1.5°C target is now out of reach**, and even 2°C is unlikely on current form. Anyone still claiming 1.5 is achievable without a miracle isn't being straight with you. Years of headlines about worst-case scenarios have also stuck in people's minds. If your reference point is Mark Lynas's *Six Degrees* from the mid-2000s, the picture really did look apocalyptic. The despair rests on real numbers, and waving it away as "just doomism" misses the point.
claims.truth: Recent projections narrow the realistic range. The latest is the **UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026**, published in October 2026: - Current policies (nothing new, nothing better): about 2.8°C by 2100. - Every current national pledge delivered: about 2.1°C. That is worse than 2024's projection of 1.9°C, "driven mainly by the US's exit from the UN climate process". - The "lowest possible overshoot" path: warming peaks at 1.7-1.8°C, with a 50% chance of falling back to 1.5°C by 2100. That needs emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, while current pledges only deliver 5-8% by 2030. So the realistic range is roughly 1.8 to 2.8°C, not 5 or 6. The extreme scenario often quoted from older modelling, labelled **RCP8.5**, is now considered implausible. None of this makes 2.1 or 2.8°C safe. Either would still mean losing most coral reefs, worse heatwaves and serious pressure on food supplies, especially in poorer countries. But it is a very different world from the "civilisation collapse" picture, and every fraction of a degree we prevent is a measurable win. There is no single global switch that flips at 1.5 or 2°C.
claims.say_this: The 5 or 6 degree scenarios aren't where we're heading any more: current policies put us at roughly 2.5 to 3 degrees by 2100, and closer to 1.8 if the net zero pledges are delivered. That's still a dangerous world, but "too late" is not the same as "nothing matters", and every tenth of a degree we shave off is a real, measurable win.

pushback.if: 1.5°C is dead, so we've already failed.
pushback.reply: Missing an exact number isn't the same as failing at the whole task. 1.7°C is meaningfully better than 1.9°C, which is meaningfully better than 2.1°C. The goal moves from "hit a specific number" to "cut emissions as fast as possible, whatever number we land near."

pushback.if: We'll hit tipping points and everything collapses anyway.
pushback.reply: Tipping points are real, and they matter for particular systems such as the Amazon, the AMOC (the Atlantic current system) and permafrost. But they are not one global switch. If anything they make the case for cutting emissions stronger, because every degree we prevent lowers the odds of setting one off.

pushback.if: So why bother, if we're still heading for 2.5°C?
pushback.reply: Because 2.5°C is what happens if we drift, and 1.8°C is what happens if we push. The gap between those two worlds decides whether coral reefs survive, whether food systems cope, and whether hundreds of millions of people can stay in their homes.

pushback.if: 1.5°C is officially over now, doesn't that prove it's too late?
pushback.reply: The UN Emissions Gap Report 2026 does say 1.5°C can now only be reached through "overshoot": going past 1.5°C for a while, then using huge amounts of mechanical and natural cooling (direct air capture, planting forests and so on) to bring temperatures back down later. **Bob Watson, former IPCC chair, calls that scenario "cuckoo land"**, because the cooling technologies it needs don't yet exist at scale. But the UN Secretary-General's view still holds: "Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible." The question has moved from "can we hit 1.5°C" to "how small and short can we keep the overshoot". That is still a debate about how much damage to avoid, and trying is still the point. See the [UN overshoot 2.8°C source](../sources/un-overshoot-2.8c-newscientist-2026.md).

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2024.
IEA World Energy Outlook 2024.

claims.claim: we'll never be able to make low-carbon cement
heard_as: Cement is impossible to decarbonise
You need limestone, so you release CO2, end of story
Cement will always be a climate problem
There's no green cement
We can't replace concrete
claims.kernel: The chemistry really is awkward. Cement is 7% of global emissions, and it's the second-most-used material on Earth after water. It's made by heating limestone (CaCO3) to a very high temperature, and that releases CO2 straight from the rock itself, before you even count the fuel used to heat the kiln. There's no way to make cement from limestone without releasing that CO2. If you focus on that one fact, "cement is impossible to decarbonise" sounds obvious.
claims.truth: Cement accounts for **7% of global greenhouse gas emissions**, more than shipping and aviation combined. For every 1 tonne of concrete, roughly 1 tonne of CO2 goes into the atmosphere. But there are three routes to cut it. Route 1 is to use less cement in concrete. Cement is one ingredient in concrete, alongside water, sand and aggregate. Europe's mix is currently about 78% cement, and many countries build safely with much less. Cutting European mixes to 50% cement by 2050 could reduce the industry's CO2 by 40%. Route 2 is carbon capture and storage (CCS): catch the CO2 as it leaves the kiln and pipe it underground. This works, and Heidelberg Cement is building the first commercial-scale plant in Norway. It does cost more: - Normal cement: about $125 per tonne - CCS cement: $100-200 per tonne extra (75-140% more, according to Gates' book) - In places with cheap energy, the extra cost could be as low as $40 per tonne - The US Inflation Reduction Act already gives an $85/tonne tax break for CO2 that is captured and stored CCS cement is expensive per tonne, but cement is a small share of what a house costs, so the effect on the finished building is very small. Route 3 is to use a different rock. Limestone contains carbon. **Calcium silicate rocks such as basalt** don't, so no CO2 is released when they're heated. The process also gives useful magnesium by-products that can absorb CO2 from the air. Brimstone has proven the concept and is building a test plant, and basalt is one of the most common rocks on Earth.
claims.say_this: Cement is hard to clean up, but it's far from impossible. There are three routes that work: put less cement in each mix, capture the CO2 at the plant, or make it from a different rock, and the extra cost barely shows on the price of a house.

pushback.if: CCS-cement is way too expensive.
pushback.reply: Per tonne of cement, yes. Per house, the extra cost is tiny, because cement is a small fraction of a house's price. Where clean energy is cheap the premium can be as low as $40/tonne, and government support, such as the US IRA's $85/tonne tax credit, closes most of the gap.

pushback.if: Basalt cement is a lab experiment.
pushback.reply: Brimstone has proven the concept and is building a test plant. That's the stage lab-grown meat was at 10 years ago. Ten years ago, most people thought CCS was the only real option for cement. The list has grown since then.

pushback.if: You can't rebuild every cement plant.
pushback.reply: You don't have to. Using less cement in every mix (route 1) cuts 40% on its own, with no new technology, only a change to building rules. Plants that keep running can be fitted with CCS (route 2), and new plants in basalt regions can use route 3.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Bill Gates, *How to Avoid a Climate Disaster*
IEA, Cement industry decarbonisation roadmap

claims.claim: we'll never be able to make low-carbon steel
heard_as: You can't make steel without coal
Steel is impossible to decarbonise
Green steel is a fantasy
It costs too much to compete
There's not enough hydrogen
We'll always need coking coal
claims.kernel: About two-thirds of the world's steel is made with coal (strictly, with "coke", which is made from coal). That has been true for more than a century, and anyone who works in steel knows coal is at the centre of it. If you frame the problem as "steel needs coal", cleaning it up sounds impossible. But coal isn't there because steel physically requires it. It's there because it strips the oxygen out of iron ore, and hydrogen can do the same job without producing CO2. The hard part is scale and cost, not the technology.
claims.truth: Steel causes **7% of global greenhouse gas emissions**. About ⅔ of the world's steel is made with coke from coal, and the remaining ⅓ is recycled scrap melted in electric arc furnaces. Each tonne of new steel burns about 0.8 tonnes of coal, which accounts for most of the emissions. There are two proven ways to remove the coal. The first is hydrogen: it strips oxygen from iron ore just as coal does, but the by-product is water (H2O) rather than CO2. It needs clean hydrogen to work. The second is direct electrification, using electricity instead of burning coal. A third option, fitting carbon capture to existing plants, also works but costs more. The scale is large but manageable: - 1 tonne of green steel needs about 4 MWh of electricity - Making the world's 1.3 billion tonnes of steel this way would need 5,200 TWh, about ⅕ of the world's electricity generation today - Total investment needed worldwide is about €1.3 trillion, or €50 billion/year over 25 years (H2 Green Steel figures) The extra cost is small once the steel is in a finished product: - Green steel: about 25% more per tonne - A $25,000 car: about $150 more (0.5-1%) - A $250,000 house: about $400 more (0.2%) - An offshore wind turbine: 0.5-2% more Several companies are already building it. H2 Green Steel has a plant under construction in Sweden, with government support. ArcelorMittal is converting a Spanish plant to hydrogen, also with government support. Boston Metal, backed by Microsoft, uses direct electrification and expects its first plant in 2026. Most European steel companies have committed to cutting emissions by 30-50% or more by 2030.
claims.say_this: We already know how to make green steel: use hydrogen instead of coal, or run the process on electricity, and the first big plants are being built now in Sweden, Spain and the US. It costs about 25% more per tonne, but that's roughly $150 on a car and $400 on a house.

pushback.if: Green steel is a lab curiosity.
pushback.reply: Not any more. H2 Green Steel's Boden plant is under construction, Boston Metal's first plant is expected in 2026, and ArcelorMittal has committed billions to hydrogen conversion. These are commercial-scale projects, not lab demonstrations.

pushback.if: It needs too much electricity.
pushback.reply: 5,200 TWh is about a fifth of current world generation, which is a lot. But a 25% rise in global electricity demand over 25 years fits the growth the grid is already planning for EVs and heat pumps. It's part of the transition rather than something blocking it.

pushback.if: 25% more expensive means nobody buys it.
pushback.reply: The effect on finished products is tiny. A car maker paying 25% more for its steel raises car prices by less than 1%, and buyers won't notice. What counts is car makers asking for green steel, because their own Scope 3 targets (emissions in their supply chain) require it.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
H2 Green Steel, Boden plant technical documentation
Boston Metal, direct electrification process
IEA, Iron and Steel Roadmap

claims.claim: meat substitutes are too expensive
heard_as: Fake meat is a luxury product
Plant burgers cost twice as much
Vegan food is only for people who can afford it
Lab meat will always be more expensive than real meat
Green food is a rich person's thing
Substitutes aren't at price parity
claims.kernel: For some products it's true. Plant-based bacon does cost more than pork bacon in UK supermarkets, and plant burgers can cost noticeably more than beef burgers. Anyone who has bought both has seen it. The step too far is going from "some plant products cost more" to "plant substitutes are unaffordable", because the picture varies a lot from product to product.
claims.truth: Comparing **UK supermarket prices per kg**: - Chicken and plant-based chicken overlap heavily, and some plant versions are cheaper - Plant and meat mince overlap in price - Plant and meat sausages overlap too - Burgers overlap a little, but plant burgers can cost noticeably more - Plant-based bacon tends to cost more than pork bacon - Fish is one of the more expensive meats either way So plant-based substitutes aren't always more expensive, but on average they still cost more than the meat they replace, mainly because of bacon and burgers. Lab-grown (cultivated) meat is on a steep downward price curve. In 2013 it cost about $2.4 million per kg. Today it's roughly $10-100 per kg, about 50,000× cheaper in around 10 years. The cost keeps falling along a curve similar to solar, wind and batteries. It still has to fall further to compete with chicken, and a lot further to compete with cheap beef. There are two ways to close the gap: make substitutes cheaper, or make meat reflect its true cost. Making substitutes cheaper is the more realistic of the two.
claims.say_this: For chicken, mince and sausages the plant versions already cost about the same as meat in UK supermarkets, though bacon and burgers are still pricier. And lab-grown meat has got 50,000× cheaper since 2013, so the gap is closing.

pushback.if: Just tax meat to level the price.
pushback.reply: That is politically very hard. UK surveys show only about 1 in 5 people support a meat tax. The 2021 UK National Food Strategy consultation found it was the least popular of all its ideas, and it split the panel members. A meat tax could also hurt the roughly **3 billion people worldwide who can't currently afford a full healthy diet**.

pushback.if: Nothing will change unless meat gets more expensive.
pushback.reply: There's another route. Moving existing farm subsidies away from meat and dairy and towards plant proteins would shift prices in a similar way to a meat tax. It tends to be easier to accept, because it isn't a new tax, only public money spent differently.

pushback.if: Lab-grown meat is a fantasy for the rich.
pushback.reply: At $10-100/kg it's still expensive, but its cost has fallen faster than any food technology in memory. It looks like solar's path: early buyers pay high prices, then larger-scale production brings costs down steeply. The bigger obstacle now is **regulation** rather than cost. Singapore and the US have approved cultivated meat for people, the UK allows it only in pet food, and Italy and some US states have banned it outright.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
UK National Food Strategy (2021)

claims.claim: meat substitutes are ultra-processed junk food
heard_as: Beyond Meat is ultra-processed junk
Fake meat is worse for your health
Veggie burgers are just junk food
Real meat is more natural
Impossible Burger is basically Coke
You should just eat vegetables, not processed alternatives
claims.kernel: "Ultra-processed" has a bad reputation, and for good reason: eating a lot of it is linked to obesity, diabetes, cancer and heart disease. Plant-based meats do meet the technical definition. They have many ingredients and they're made in factories, so it's easy to lump them in with everything else. The catch is that "ultra-processed" covers very different foods, and the evidence points to the harm coming from particular groups, processed meats and sugary drinks, rather than from all processed food equally.
claims.truth: Compared with processed meat, meat substitutes usually have fewer calories, less total fat and less saturated fat, and more fibre. Some match a beef burger's 20-25 g of protein per serving, while others come in lower, at around 15 g. Protein quality is worth knowing about: animal foods contain the full range of amino acids, while plant foods often need combining, which a varied plant diet does easily. Substitutes can fall short on calcium, zinc and vitamin B12 unless they're fortified, and many products now are. A typical "ultra-processed" checklist has 8 markers: | Criteria | Processed meat | Plant-based meat | |---|---|---| | Convenient | ✅ | ✅ | | High in calories | ✅ | ❌ | | High in sugar | ❌ | ❌ | | High in saturated fat | ✅ | ❌ | | High in salt | ✅ | ❌ | | Many ingredients | ✅ | ✅ | | Low in fibre | ✅ | ❌ | | Couldn't be made in a normal kitchen | ✅ | ✅ | Plant-based meat ticks **3 of 8** markers, and processed meat ticks 6 of 8. On the markers that matter for health, they aren't in the same group. High overall consumption of ultra-processed food is linked to obesity, diabetes, cancer and heart disease. But when researchers look inside the category, the foods doing the damage are processed meats and sugary drinks. Other ultra-processed foods, including meat substitutes, show no link to higher disease risk, and some studies even find a lower risk. Eating more plant-based protein is linked to better health and a lower risk of dying early.
claims.say_this: Technically they're ultra-processed, but the ultra-processed foods linked to disease are mainly processed meats and sugary drinks, not veggie burgers. Plant-based meats are usually lower in calories, saturated fat and salt, and higher in fibre, than the meat they replace.

pushback.if: But they're still ultra-processed.
pushback.reply: Yes, technically. But the category is very mixed. A veggie burger and a can of Coke both meet the definition, yet they behave very differently in the body. The health harms come from calorie density, saturated fat, salt, low fibre and specific ingredients such as the nitrates in processed meat, and meat substitutes don't score badly on those.

pushback.if: Cows are natural, factories aren't.
pushback.reply: Being natural isn't a measure of nutrition. Much of what goes into a beef burger also passes through a factory: mincing, stabilisers, packaging. What matters is what's inside the food, not where it was put together.

pushback.if: What about processing damaging the food?
pushback.reply: That's a fair concern. Some processing does affect nutrition, for example very high heat, very long processing or chemical solvents. Modern extrusion and mycoprotein processes keep most of the nutritional value, though not all. If it worries you, tofu, tempeh and plain beans and lentils are the reference point: cheaper and healthier than most substitutes, though less convenient.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
NOVA food classification (Monteiro et al., São Paulo)
Cochrane and BMJ reviews of ultra-processed food consumption and disease outcomes

claims.claim: meat substitutes are worse for the climate because they're processed
heard_as: Beyond Meat is worse than a real steak
Processed food has a bigger footprint
The energy in fake meat cancels the benefit
Lab-grown meat is worse than beef
Impossible Burgers aren't really green
Factory food is climate-heavy
claims.kernel: Factory-made food does use energy: running fermenters, heating, packaging, refrigerated transport. That shows up as emissions. It feels natural to think that food grown on a farm must be lower carbon than food made in a factory. What that leaves out is how much land and methane goes into raising livestock, which is far bigger than any factory's energy use.
claims.truth: Hannah Ritchie compares emissions **per 100 g of protein** across the whole supply chain, from farming to processing and packaging: - Beef and lamb are by far the highest-emitting protein sources on the planet - Pork is lower than beef and lamb, but still very high - Meat substitutes (Impossible Burger, Beyond Meat, tofu, Quorn/mycoprotein, peas) all cause much lower emissions than beef and lamb, often more than 10× lower than pork - Substitutes also beat most chicken and egg production, and only the most efficient chicken farms come close - Lab-grown (cultivated) meat is lower than beef and roughly similar to chicken - Even against the most climate-friendly beef and pork farms (not the average ones), substitutes win almost every time - Plain plant foods (peas, beans, lentils) beat processed substitutes, but the substitutes still beat any meat
claims.say_this: Factories do use energy, but meat substitutes still cause far less carbon than meat, often more than ten times less than pork and much less than beef or lamb. Beans and peas are better still, but substitutes beat even the most climate-friendly beef farms.

pushback.if: But they use so much electricity to make.
pushback.reply: They do, but it's small next to the methane from cattle and sheep. Livestock emissions are dominated by methane from digestion and by land-use change from clearing forest for pasture. The factory energy behind a plant burger is a small addition compared with what a cow burps out over its life.

pushback.if: But I read lab-grown meat could be 25× worse than beef.
pushback.reply: That headline came from a study that assumed a **biopharmaceutical-style production method**, an unusual and energy-hungry way of making lab meat that the industry doesn't plan to use. Standard cultivated-meat processes are much lower carbon than beef, even on today's fossil-heavy grid, and far better again on solar or wind.

pushback.if: Are substitutes really better than the best beef?
pushback.reply: Yes, in almost every case. Even the most climate-efficient beef farms emit more per 100 g of protein than a plant burger. The gap between the best beef and average beef is real, but both sit above substitutes.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Poore & Nemecek, *Science*, 2018. Food carbon footprints per unit of protein

claims.claim: we'll just swap fossil fuel dependency for mineral dependency
heard_as: We'd just depend on China instead of the Middle East
Rare earths are the new oil
It's a bad trade, one dependency for another
China controls the transition
Mineral dependency is worse than fossil fuel dependency
We're going to get held hostage by Beijing
claims.kernel: The concentration figures are stark. China refines 80% of the world's rare earths, and the DRC mines 70% of its cobalt. Lithium is concentrated in Australia and South America. Put that way, it sounds as though we'd simply be depending on China instead of Saudi Arabia. What that misses is that fossil fuel dependency is about keeping the system running, while mineral dependency is about building it.
claims.truth: Mining is concentrated in a few countries: - More than 70% of cobalt is mined in the DRC - More than 60% of rare earths and graphite are produced in China - More than 70% of platinum comes from South Africa Refining is even more concentrated. China refines more than 80% of the world's rare earths, dominates the refining of cobalt, lithium and copper, and also leads in making the finished products, batteries and EVs. Fossil fuel dependency is a bigger problem for far more people. **86% of the world's population** live in countries that import fossil fuels, which leaves them exposed to supply shocks. Only 14% live in countries that export them. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, up to 50,000 people across Europe died from cold and energy poverty, and high energy prices pushed food prices up too, through the cost of fertiliser. Renewables change that picture. If the world ran on renewables, 92% of the world's population would live in countries with enough sun or wind to cover at least 10× their own energy needs. Only 8% would have limited renewable resources.
claims.say_this: Mineral supply is concentrated, but it's a different kind of risk: if someone cuts off your gas, the heating stops today, whereas if they cut off your minerals, the solar panels and turbines you already have keep working. You just can't build new ones for a while, and nobody can switch off the sun.

pushback.if: So we'd just be dependent on China instead of Saudi Arabia.
pushback.reply: For the next stage of building, partly yes. But once the panels and turbines are installed, nobody can cut off the sun or the wind. Fossil fuels need an unbroken supply chain forever. Minerals need one only while we build.

pushback.if: China could weaponise rare earths.
pushback.reply: It tried briefly in the 2010 dispute with Japan. Prices spiked, and the world responded by finding sources outside China, so reserves and refining capacity elsewhere grew fast. Rare earths are harder to control than oil because they're found in many places. They just aren't refined in many places.

pushback.if: But we still need to build a lot for decades.
pushback.reply: Yes, which is why spreading supply matters. The US, Australia, Norway, Sweden and Portugal are all developing new mining and refining capacity. Norway recently discovered Europe's largest rare-earth deposit. The **US Inflation Reduction Act** is putting significant money into processing minerals at home. And AI-driven mineral discovery (KoBold Metals, HyperSpectral) is making new deposits easier to find. This is a supply problem that can be solved, not a trap.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA, Critical Minerals reports
EU Critical Raw Materials Act (2023)

claims.claim: There aren't enough minerals in the world to build all this
heard_as: we'll run out of lithium
there isn't enough copper for the grid
peak minerals
claims.kernel: Clean technology does use more minerals. The IEA notes that a typical electric car needs about six times the mineral inputs of a conventional one, and an onshore wind plant about nine times more than a gas plant.
claims.truth: Using more minerals isn't the same as running out. The Energy Transitions Commission found no fundamental shortage of key materials: known geological resources exceed projected demand out to 2050. Demand for critical minerals roughly triples by 2030, to around **30 million tonnes a year**. Compare that with the roughly 15 billion tonnes of fossil fuels extracted every year now. A 2023 study in Joule put total demand to 2050 at up to 1.96 billion tonnes of steel, 241 million tonnes of aluminium and 82 million tonnes of copper, small fractions of accessible reserves. It found annual production would not need to grow by more than 20% for supply to meet demand. And unlike coal, these materials can be recovered and used again.
claims.say_this: We dig up about 15 billion tonnes of fossil fuel every year and set fire to it. The transition needs around 30 million tonnes of minerals a year, and you can use those again.

pushback.if: But the mines don't exist yet
pushback.reply: That's the real constraint, and it's about permits and investment timelines, not geology. It's worth arguing about, but it's a different argument.

sources.label: MIT Technology Review, busting materials myths.
IEA, critical minerals in clean energy transitions.

claims.claim: All that mining is worse for the planet than fossil fuels
heard_as: child labour in cobalt mines
lithium mining destroys the environment
it's just swapping one extraction for another
claims.kernel: Mining causes real environmental and social harm: it uses water, destroys habitat, and some supply chains involve serious human rights abuses. Anyone raising this is right about that part, and it's fair to say so.
claims.truth: The comparison still doesn't hold. Even counting waste rock, the energy transition involves less material extraction than today's fossil fuel economy. The biggest difference is that it's a **one-time build**. A wind turbine's materials are dug up once, installed, and can later be recycled. Coal, oil and gas have to be extracted and burned continuously, forever. Fossil fuel extraction isn't clean or free of human rights problems either. It's simply older and talked about less.
claims.say_this: Mining does real harm and that should be fixed. The difference is you mine for a turbine once, and you mine for a coal plant every single day it runs.

pushback.if: So you accept the harm as long as it's green
pushback.reply: No. Push for traceable supply chains and recycling. That fight is worth having, and it isn't a reason to burn more gas in the meantime.

sources.label: MIT Technology Review, busting materials myths.
Hannah Ritchie, energy transition materials.

claims.claim: there isn't enough clean energy to replace fossil fuels
heard_as: Renewables can't replace fossil fuels
There isn't enough solar and wind to power the world
The sun doesn't shine at night
It's physically impossible to run everything on renewables
We'd need to cover the whole planet in solar panels
Clean energy is too small to matter
claims.kernel: At first glance the numbers look enormous. The world uses hundreds of exajoules of energy every year, and if all of that has to come from solar panels and wind turbines, it sounds impossible on any human timescale. The trouble is that this measures the target in "primary energy": the total energy that goes in, including everything lost as heat. That measure was designed for a world that burns fuel, not one that runs on electricity.
claims.truth: Burning fuel is very wasteful, and the alternatives are far more efficient: - A coal power plant turns about one third of its energy into electricity, and the rest is lost as heat up the chimney. Gas power wastes about half. Solar and wind waste almost nothing. - So **1 unit of solar or wind can replace 2 to 3 units of coal**. A city needing 100 TWh of electricity would burn 300 TWh of coal to get it, or 200 TWh of gas, or need just 100 TWh of solar and wind. - Petrol cars are only about 20% efficient: 80 cents of every €1 of petrol becomes waste heat. Electric cars are about 80% efficient, so driving an EV uses only a quarter to a third of the energy of a petrol car. - If the world electrified everything that can be electrified (cars, heating, industry, short flights, ferries), total world energy demand would fall by around 40%, from about 416 EJ today to about 247 EJ (Ritchie 2024), even as electricity demand rises. - Renewables are already doing most of the new work. Between 2010 and 2022 they supplied 57% of the growth in global electricity, and in 2022 alone they supplied 92% of new demand.
claims.say_this: We don't have to match today's fossil fuel use one-for-one, because burning fuel wastes most of its energy as heat, so one unit of solar or wind can replace two to three units of coal. If we electrify cars, heating and industry, total world energy demand actually falls by about 40%, even as electricity use goes up.

pushback.if: But electricity demand is going up, that proves it isn't working.
pushback.reply: Rising electricity demand is exactly what you'd expect if the transition is working. Cars, heat pumps and industry are moving off gas and petrol and onto the grid. It's **total** energy demand that falls. Electricity is the visible part of a much bigger efficiency gain that mostly goes unseen.

pushback.if: OK, but poor countries will need much more energy as they develop.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that's right and fair. Rich countries will use less and poorer countries will use more, but the world total still falls, because moving away from burning fuel saves so much energy. The two don't conflict.

pushback.if: You're leaving out storage, solar and wind are intermittent.
pushback.reply: Not quite. The first 70 to 80% of a power system can be covered by solar and wind plus a modest amount of storage. The last 20 to 30% is harder in regions with little sun and wind, and needs other tools: nuclear, hydro, geothermal, batteries, and gas as a shrinking backup. That's a real engineering problem, but it's very different from there not being enough clean energy at all.

sources.label: IEA, Global electricity generation, 2010-2022
Bloomberg NEF, New Energy Outlook 2024 (renewable share of new demand)

claims.claim: there aren't enough EV chargers
heard_as: There are no chargers where I live
I can never find a working charger
Charging is a nightmare
The infrastructure isn't there
It's not built out enough yet
You can't rely on public chargers
Rural areas are being left behind
claims.kernel: In a lot of places it's true. If you live in a city flat with no off-street parking, and the nearest public charger is a mile away, often broken, or priced like petrol, "there aren't enough chargers" is a reasonable complaint. Surveys of over 31,000 EV drivers across 15 countries keep finding that charger availability is their top concern, and **41% of would-be buyers say they'd only switch if chargers were as easy to find as petrol stations**.
claims.truth: - Over a million public charging points are being installed worldwide every year - The EU's charging network tripled in three years and is ahead of its own targets - The global average in 2023 was **10 EVs per public charger**, but that hides huge variation: - New Zealand: 88 EVs per charger (thin network) - South Korea: 3 EVs per charger (dense network) - The EVs-per-charger figure leaves out how fast each charger is (a fast charger serves more cars a day than a slow one), and where people actually charge (most charge at home) Where people charge matters more than the public numbers suggest: - Only about 5% of Americans rely mainly on public chargers - In the UK, about 20% rely mainly on public chargers - 70% of UK homes have off-street parking where they could charge, but only 30% of city EV drivers have that option - About 30% of UK drivers charge at work Even the oil industry is joining in: Shell and others are installing chargers at their own petrol stations.
claims.say_this: It depends where you live, but over a million public chargers are going in worldwide every year and the EU has tripled its network in three years. The real gaps are for people who can't charge at home, and chargers that don't work when you get there.

pushback.if: There are barely any chargers on the motorway.
pushback.reply: It depends on the country. In much of Western Europe, rapid chargers on motorways are now common. In North America and the UK the gaps are smaller than they were three years ago. Where the network is thin, that's a real problem, and the answer is targeted investment.

pushback.if: Half the ones I've tried are broken.
pushback.reply: Reliability is the specific problem inside the wider one. The share of chargers that actually work matters more than how many are installed, and some networks are known for downtime. Rules on uptime and on being able to pay the same way everywhere would fix more than building extra chargers.

pushback.if: I live in a flat with no driveway, and rapid chargers are expensive.
pushback.reply: This is the clearest unfairness in the EV story. Fixing it needs **street-side and neighbourhood charging** for people without garages, priced closer to the cost of charging at home than to rapid-charger rates. It's a policy problem, not a physics problem.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA, Global EV Outlook 2024

claims.claim: there isn't enough land for everyone to go plant-based
heard_as: There isn't enough land for everyone to eat plants
Vegan diets would need more land
We can't grow enough vegetables for everyone
Grazing land would go to waste
The math doesn't work for a plant-based world
Cows use land we can't use anyway
claims.kernel: It makes intuitive sense. If you swap meat for vegetables, surely you need lots of extra vegetable fields? There's also a feeling that grazing land would be wasted if it stopped producing meat. Both thoughts are reasonable. What they miss is that most cropland is already growing food, just food for animals rather than for us.
claims.truth: About three-quarters of the world's farmland goes to livestock: grazing land plus the cropland that grows animal feed. That comes to **75% of all farmland on Earth**. Where the crops go: - Only half of the world's cereal crops go directly to human food. - 75% of the world's soybeans are fed to animals, not people. - Tofu, tempeh and soy milk use only 7% of world soy (about 20% if you include soybean oil). Animals are poor at turning feed into food: - Feed a cow 100 calories and you get 3 calories back as meat or milk. - Feed a pig 100 calories and you get 9 back. - Feed a chicken 100 calories and you get 13 back. Animals give us about 37% of our calories but eat most of the crops. The modelling Ritchie cites puts today's diet at about 4 billion hectares of farmland. A fully plant-based diet would need about **1 billion hectares**. That's a 75% cut. Grazing land is a separate story. Two-thirds of the world's grazing land can't grow crops anyway, because the soil, terrain or climate isn't suitable. So it isn't wasted, but it also can't easily become cropland.
claims.say_this: It's actually the other way round: eating more plants needs less land, because most farmland today grows food for animals, not people. A fully vegan world would need about 1 billion hectares of farmland instead of today's 4 billion, a 75% drop, and even a moderate shift by everyone would save a lot.

pushback.if: But what about the land the animals graze on?
pushback.reply: Two-thirds of it can't grow crops anyway, and grazing is a sensible use of that land. The real saving is the arable land that grows soy and maize for animals, which could grow food for people directly.

pushback.if: Everyone going vegan is unrealistic.
pushback.reply: Agreed, and Ritchie says so herself. She doesn't argue for 100% vegan. A moderate cut in meat and dairy across the whole world would matter more than a small group of people going fully vegan.

pushback.if: You'd need vast new fields of vegetables.
pushback.reply: Some, yes: we'd need more fruit and vegetables. But the drop in animal-feed cropland is much larger, so total farmland falls. Under a full dietary shift, the [EAT-Lancet](../sectors/agriculture-food/eat-lancet-planetary-diet-2025.md) modelling shows total agricultural land falling by about 3.4 million km², an area the size of India.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Poore & Nemecek (2018), *Science*. Global food-system land use

claims.claim: there isn't enough public support to tackle climate change
heard_as: Nobody cares about climate change any more
The public won't accept it
There's no political will
People say they care but they don't act
Everyone's too busy with the cost of living to care about climate
Support has collapsed since the pandemic
It's a niche issue
claims.kernel: The news makes it feel as if nobody agrees on anything. Every week brings a climate protest and a backlash, an oil lobbyist and a Greta Thunberg quote, a viral post from a denier and another from a doomer. If most of what you see comes from X, cable news or partisan headlines, it looks like a 50-50 shouting match. Some politicians and industry executives repeat that framing because it suits them: if the public is split, doing nothing looks defensible.
claims.truth: Large international surveys keep finding big majorities for climate action, country after country. - A 63-country survey of 59,000 people found **86% think humans are causing climate change** and see it as a serious threat. Nearly three quarters back specific policies such as carbon taxes, more public transport, renewables, EV chargers and airline taxes. - A 125-country survey of 130,000 people found 89% want more political action, and 86% think people in their country should try to fight climate change. - In the United States, often assumed to be the outlier, 74% think the US should join international climate action and 71% say climate change is already harming Americans. - In the European Union, 93% see climate change as a serious problem, and over two-thirds think their government is not doing enough. - The share who want their government to do more ranges from 97% in China down to 62% in Finland. Most countries are above 80%. The bigger issue is the perception gap. Asked how many others support climate action, people guess about half the real number. Americans guessed that roughly a third supported it, when the real figure is around two thirds. Climate supporters think they're in the minority, when in almost every country they're the majority.
claims.say_this: Most people in every country surveyed want climate action: about 86% agree humans are causing climate change and around 89% want more political action. The catch is that we all underestimate how many others agree with us, so the silent majority thinks it's the minority.

pushback.if: If people really supported action, they'd vote for it.
pushback.reply: They often do, but party politics rarely reflects the size of that majority. When climate is on the ballot as a specific proposal, such as in California or several EU referenda, it usually wins. When it's bundled with other issues, party loyalty tends to decide the result.

pushback.if: Support is one thing, willingness to pay is another.
pushback.reply: That's fair, and it's a real tension. But the surveys also ask about specific policies like carbon taxes, airline levies and home retrofits, and majorities still back them, especially when the policy protects lower-income households. What people reject is being asked to pay while a few at the top pay nothing.

pushback.if: The US is different.
pushback.reply: Less than you'd think. 74% of Americans support the US joining international climate action, and 71% say Americans are already being harmed by climate change. What stands out in the US is the gap between public opinion and political outcomes, rather than the level of support.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

Andre P., Boneva T., Chopra F., Falk A. (2024) *Globally representative evidence on the actual and perceived support for climate action*, *Nature Climate Change*. The 130,000-person, 125-country survey
Sparkman G., Geiger N., Weber E. (2022), *Nature Communications*. Pluralistic ignorance about climate support
Yale Program on Climate Change Communication. Climate Opinion Maps

claims.claim: nuclear power takes too long to build to matter for the climate
heard_as: Nuclear is too slow to matter
It's already too late for nuclear
Solar is faster and cheaper
Hinkley Point proves nuclear is impossible
By the time it's built the climate crisis will be worse
We don't have time for nuclear
claims.kernel: The Western examples really are bad. Construction of **Hinkley Point C** in the UK started in 2017, and it now looks unlikely to produce power before 2031: at least 14 years for the first unit. Flamanville in France started in 2007 and only opened in 2024, more than a decade late. Both are poor advertisements for nuclear just when climate policy needs speed. Looking at those two projects and concluding nuclear is too slow is a reasonable reaction.
claims.truth: Those Western projects are outliers. Data on over 600 nuclear plants built since 1950 shows: - Around **80% took less than a decade** to build - 1 in 5 took less than 5 years - The global average construction time is 6 to 8 years China and South Korea are building at about 5-7 years per plant today. India is building too, more slowly. Nearly all US and EU plants are over 30 years old, because those countries largely stopped building. Restarting from cold makes everything slow. Ritchie points to four reasons the West is slow. Almost every Western plant is a one-off design, so there is no learning curve. Regulations change partway through construction, and each design change costs a great deal of time and money. The skilled workforce has gone, because the UK and France stopped building and the expertise retired. And big, complex construction projects tend to overrun in general, with nuclear at the harder end.
claims.say_this: Western nuclear plants often take over a decade because we stopped building them for 30 years and had to relearn how, but countries that build regularly, like China, South Korea and India, do it in five to eight. Nuclear won't outpace solar and wind, but "too slow" describes recent Western projects, not what's possible.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are faster to build, why bother with nuclear?
pushback.reply: They are faster, and most new capacity will be renewable. But grids in northern countries with weak winter sun still need steady low-carbon backup, and nuclear is one of the few options. It works alongside solar and wind rather than against them.

pushback.if: The Hinkley Point disaster proves the whole industry is broken.
pushback.reply: Hinkley is a bad advertisement, but it isn't typical. It's a first-of-its-kind design in a country that hadn't built for 20 years. The lesson is to build the same design many times in a row, keep the rules stable, and keep the workforce employed between projects.

pushback.if: We don't have time to wait 8 years.
pushback.reply: An 8-year build starting today finishes in the mid-2030s, which is still useful. Renewables can handle near-term growth while nuclear plants under construction come online to replace retiring fossil fuel plants.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA. Nuclear plant age and construction data

claims.claim: nuclear power is too dangerous
heard_as: Nuclear is dangerous
Remember Chernobyl / Fukushima
One accident would kill millions
Nuclear radiation causes cancer
We can't take the risk
The people who lived near Fukushima are all sick
claims.kernel: Chernobyl and Fukushima are fixed in public memory, and any nuclear accident is sudden, dramatic and filmed. Chernobyl even became a Netflix series. Fossil fuel deaths happen quietly and spread out: air pollution kills 11,000 to 22,000 people every single day, and none of them make the news. If your picture of nuclear comes from those accidents, it's natural to overestimate the risk.
claims.truth: Deaths per terawatt-hour of electricity generated (Markandya & Wilkinson, Sovacool, UNSCEAR): | Energy source | Deaths per TWh | |---|---| | Brown coal | 33 | | Coal | 25 | | Gas | 2.8 | | Hydro | 1.3 | | Wind, Solar, Nuclear | <0.1 each | Nuclear causes **more than 99% fewer deaths than coal** and about 98% fewer than gas. Wind, nuclear and solar are so close in the data that they can't be ranked with confidence, but all three are far safer than fossil fuels. The major accidents, counted in full: - Three Mile Island (1979, level 5): zero deaths. - Fukushima (2011, level 7): no one died directly in the disaster, and there were about 40-50 injuries. One later cancer death is disputed. Around 2,313 premature deaths came from the evacuation, mostly elderly people displaced and cut off from healthcare, for a total of about 2,314. Studies of the wider population find no measurable increase in cancer. - Chernobyl (1986, level 7): the confirmed direct toll is under 100. A reasonable broader estimate is 300 to 500 deaths. Higher WHO figures, up to 4,000 long-term deaths, are now considered too high, and UNSCEAR follow-ups found no solid evidence of higher cancer rates in the wider population. Even taking the highest figure of 4,000 across all of nuclear history, coal air pollution kills more people every single week.
claims.say_this: Nuclear isn't risk-free, but for the electricity it makes it kills hundreds of times fewer people than coal or gas, about the same as solar and wind. The quiet danger is the fossil fuel system it could replace, whose air pollution kills 4 to 8 million people a year.

pushback.if: You can't compare a rare huge accident with steady day-to-day deaths.
pushback.reply: You can, and you have to, because both are real. Fossil fuel deaths aren't less real for being quiet. If you only count dramatic events, you end up preferring the system that kills more people overall.

pushback.if: What about the next Chernobyl?
pushback.reply: A future accident isn't impossible, especially as more plants are built. The answer is safer reactor designs and sensible siting, rather than sticking with fossil fuels that are killing millions today.

pushback.if: Nuclear plants are terrorism targets.
pushback.reply: Modern containment structures are extremely hard to breach. Hydro dams would also be catastrophic if attacked. The answer is good security, not giving up the technology.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Markandya A. & Wilkinson P. (2007), *The Lancet*. Deaths per TWh
Sovacool B. et al. (2016). Energy accident review
UNSCEAR (2008, 2018). UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation

claims.claim: nuclear power is too expensive
heard_as: Nuclear is uneconomic
Hinkley Point C cost £30 billion
Solar is way cheaper
You'd never build nuclear if you had to compete
Nuclear only survives on subsidies
Nobody would invest in nuclear without government backing
claims.kernel: The Western numbers are eye-watering. **Vogtle 3 and 4** in the US are expected to cost at least $6,000 per kilowatt, a sixfold jump from 1960s US plants at about $1,000/kW. Hinkley Point C in the UK is one of the most expensive infrastructure projects in British history. Over the same period, solar and wind costs have dropped 80-90%. Put a Western nuclear figure next to a solar farm bid and it's easy to conclude nuclear can't compete.
claims.truth: Cost per megawatt built since 2000 (Britain Remade / Dumitriu & Hopkinson data, £m per MW): | Country | £m per MW | |---|---| | South Korea | £2.24 | | India | £2.26 | | China | £2.37 | | Japan | £2.67 | | France | £4.43 | | Finland | £5.97 | | UK | £9.42 | | USA | £10.23 | The US and UK are **4-5 times more expensive** than South Korea. Wages in the UK and South Korea are similar, so labour costs can't explain a fivefold gap. The real causes lie in how projects are run. They run late, and delays cost money: labour makes up about 80% of typical cost overruns on delayed nuclear projects. Regulations keep changing, and a design change mid-build ripples through the whole project. And plants aren't built repeatedly. The US has about 50 reactors, nearly all decades old, and the US Department of Energy estimates you'd need to build at least 20 identical plants to find the real steady-state cost. That hasn't happened.
claims.say_this: Nuclear is expensive in the US and UK, no argument there, but South Korea builds plants for about a fifth of the US price, and China and India are close behind. The high cost comes from stop-start building, shifting rules and one-off designs, so countries that build steadily build cheaply.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are much cheaper. Why bother?
pushback.reply: They are cheaper, and most new capacity will be renewable. But grids in northern countries need steady low-carbon backup. The first 70-80% of a grid from solar and wind is cheap, while the last 20-30% is expensive, especially through winters with little sun and wind. For that last slice, nuclear plus storage might work out cheaper than solar and wind with huge amounts of long-duration storage.

pushback.if: Once built, isn't it also expensive to run?
pushback.reply: No, running costs are low. Fuel is a small share of nuclear costs, and a plant produces power for 40-60 years once built, whereas fossil fuel plants keep buying fuel for their whole life. The expensive part is construction.

pushback.if: The West has proven it can't do this cheaply.
pushback.reply: For now, yes, but that comes from decades of not building. South Korea and China have shown you can build in the £2-3m/MW range. The fixes are consistency, standard designs and stable regulation.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Sam Dumitriu and Ben Hopkinson, Britain Remade. Nuclear construction cost dataset

claims.claim: nuclear waste is an unsolved problem
heard_as: We don't know what to do with nuclear waste
Nuclear waste stays radioactive for millions of years
There's no safe place to store it
We're leaving a problem for our grandchildren
Yucca Mountain proves we can't solve this
One leak would be catastrophic
claims.kernel: "We haven't built a permanent storage site yet" is a true statement. Countries have talked about deep underground storage for decades, and until Finland's Onkalo opens, nobody can point to a working example. That gap between plan and practice feels like a hole in the safety case. It's a fair concern, but it's a different one from "we don't know what to do".
claims.truth: Nuclear waste comes in three categories, which differ a lot in volume and radioactivity: | Type | Share of volume | Share of radioactivity | |---|---|---| | Low-level (gloves, tools) | 92% | 1% | | Intermediate-level | 7% | 4% | | High-level (used fuel rods) | 1% | 95% | Low-level waste is mostly used gloves, mops and tools, and it isn't very radioactive. It's stored near the surface in concrete vaults for about 100 years, and most of its radioactivity fades within decades. Intermediate-level waste needs longer isolation in multi-layered casks. **High-level waste** is the small but serious 1%, mostly used fuel rods, and it holds 95% of the radioactivity. On high-level waste, the picture is better than many people assume: - Up to 96% of the material can be recycled into fresh nuclear fuel. France, Japan, Russia and China do this. The US doesn't, and wastes a large potential energy source. - The volume is small: about 29,000 m³ of high-level waste worldwide by 2016. Piled on a football pitch, that would be about 5 metres high, tiny next to fossil fuel waste. - Nuclear waste storage has caused zero deaths or injuries. - Nuclear is the most regulated and monitored waste industry in the world. - Coal ash contains mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium and chromium, and is often more radioactive than well-managed nuclear waste, yet it gets a fraction of the attention.
claims.say_this: We know how to store nuclear waste safely, deep underground in stable rock, and Finland is about to prove it in practice. All the high-level waste ever produced would fit on a football pitch piled 5 metres high, much of it can be recycled, and nobody has ever died from it.

pushback.if: But no country has actually built a permanent underground site.
pushback.reply: Finland has. The **Onkalo repository** is 430 metres deep, in rock tested for stability, and designed to keep waste isolated for at least 100,000 years. It's expected to open in the next few years. If it works, other countries can follow with more confidence and a real cost benchmark.

pushback.if: But the US Yucca Mountain site failed.
pushback.reply: Yes. Yucca Mountain took decades and was cancelled, mostly for political reasons. That was a failure of policy rather than physics. Finland succeeded because it handled local politics well from the start.

pushback.if: 100,000 years is a long time to guarantee safety.
pushback.reply: It is, and scientists disagree here. Direct radiation exposure becomes safe within about 1,000 years. If waste ever got into water or food, some isotopes would stay dangerous much longer, with estimates ranging from 10,000 to 1,000,000 years. Deep underground sites are designed cautiously, to cover the far end of that range.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Radioactive waste management
Posiva Oy. Onkalo repository technical documentation

claims.claim: poor countries need fossil fuels to develop
heard_as: Africa needs coal
Poor countries need fossil fuels to lift people out of poverty
It's colonial to deny them development
You can't be green when you're poor
The West did it, so should they
Energy justice means fossil fuels
claims.kernel: For 100 years it was true. Every country that industrialised did it on coal, oil and gas, because there was no serious alternative. In the 20th century, energy and fossil fuels became so tangled up that people still treat them as the same thing. There's also a real fairness point inside the claim. Rich countries burned fossil fuels for centuries to get where they are, then told poorer countries not to. That hypocrisy is real, and people are right to be wary when it comes wrapped in climate messaging.
claims.truth: Fossil fuels were the fuel of development, but it's **energy in general** that lifts people out of poverty, and the cheapest new energy is now clean. The emissions at stake are small. The 48 countries of sub-Saharan Africa (excluding South Africa) hold 14% of the world's population but produce only 0.6% of global CO2 emissions. Even if their electricity tripled and every kWh came from natural gas, world emissions would rise by only about 0.6%, while transforming people's lives. Indoor air pollution from cooking with wood and charcoal kills over 2 million people a year. A short-term switch to kerosene or gas would save lives without much harm to the climate, and clean cooking gas often goes hand in hand with electrification in the longer run. Poorer countries are well placed for clean energy. They have plenty of sun and wind, a large share of the minerals needed for batteries, and no ageing fossil fuel plants to write off, so they can build modern systems from scratch. It's already happening: - Namibia, Brazil, Chile and Morocco get a higher share of their electricity from solar and wind than the EU or the US does. - Pakistan has a rooftop solar boom, as families make their own power to cope with an unreliable grid. - South Africa shows the same pattern after repeated failures of its coal-based grid. - Kigali (Rwanda) banned new petrol motorbikes in 2025 to cut urban air pollution. The bottleneck is **capital**, not technology: - Loans for a solar plant in South Africa, India or Mexico cost about twice as much (about 12%) as in rich countries (about 5%). In low-income countries rates are higher still. - Rich countries promised $100 billion a year in climate finance to poorer countries by 2020. They missed that target by about $20 billion and only reached it years late, with some of the money simply old aid budgets relabelled as green finance. - The G7 has blocked funding for any fossil fuel project in Africa, while its own members responded to the war in Ukraine by firing up coal plants and building new LNG terminals.
claims.say_this: Poor countries need energy to develop, and today solar and wind are the cheapest new power in most of the world, so that energy doesn't have to come from fossil fuels. The real obstacle is money: they pay two to three times more than rich countries to borrow for the same clean project.

pushback.if: But some fossil fuels will still be needed.
pushback.reply: Fair. Some fossil fuel use during the transition, especially gas for cooking and industry, is expected and defensible. Nobody needs to ban all fossil fuels in poor countries. The point is that they aren't locked into fossil fuels when a cheaper, cleaner path is open, as long as the finance is there.

pushback.if: Rich countries have no right to lecture.
pushback.reply: Agreed, and that isn't the argument. The argument is that **the finance system** is what's holding poor countries back from clean energy. Rich countries can fix that by delivering the climate finance they pledged, offering fair borrowing rates and no longer blocking regional development banks. Blocking fossil fuels while offering nothing in their place is the worst of both worlds.

pushback.if: China is undercutting everyone with cheap solar and EVs.
pushback.reply: Yes, and for poorer countries that's mostly good news, because it brings down the cost of building clean energy. Rich countries can either help spread affordable Chinese clean tech or build a competing industry. Complaining about low prices doesn't help the countries that most need cheap solar.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Our World in Data. CO2 emissions by country
Climate Policy Initiative. Cost of Capital Observatory
OECD. Climate finance provided and mobilized 2013-2022
World Health Organization. Household air pollution mortality

claims.claim: It says recycled on the packaging, so plastic recycling is working
heard_as: this bottle is made from recycled plastic
the brands have sorted this out
chemical recycling solved it
claims.kernel: The label is legally accurate, which is what makes this one hard to spot. Nobody is lying outright, and it's reasonable to trust what the packet says.
claims.truth: It works through an accounting method called **mass balance**. A manufacturer spreads a small amount of recycled feedstock across a whole production system on paper, then labels individual products as recycled, even when the item in your hand is around 95% virgin naphtha (new plastic made from oil). A 2026 Guardian and IJ4EU investigation found products from Kraft Heinz and Mondelez carrying recycled claims on this basis. The EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation makes the approach legal in 2026 rather than closing the loophole.
claims.say_this: "Recycled" on the label often means the company bought some recycled material somewhere in its system, not that it's in the packet in your hand. And the rules allow it.

pushback.if: So should I stop recycling?
pushback.reply: No, keep recycling. Just don't treat a recycled label as proof, and push for reuse and less packaging, which is where the bigger gains are.

sources.label: The Guardian / IJ4EU, mass balance investigation, January 2026.

claims.claim: Renewables can't keep the lights on when the wind stops
heard_as: you need baseload power
what happens on a still winter night
we'll always need gas as backup
claims.kernel: Wind and solar really are variable, and a grid has to balance supply and demand every second, so the worry makes sense. Grid operators take it seriously, which is why they plan for it rather than dismiss it.
claims.truth: There's no single fix. Variability is managed with a mix of tools: spreading wind and solar farms over a wide area, interconnection between countries, storage, and shifting flexible demand to windy hours. Grid-scale batteries now respond faster than gas plants can, and their costs have fallen steeply. Ireland already runs large shares of its electricity on wind for long periods. The last stretch to a fully reliable zero-carbon grid is hard and still being worked out. The **first 70 or 80%** is a solved engineering problem, and it's being built today.
claims.say_this: Grid operators handle this with links between countries, storage and shifting demand. The last stretch is hard, but the first three quarters is being built right now.

pushback.if: So you admit you need gas backup
pushback.reply: For now, some. The question is how fast that shrinks, rather than whether renewables work. Nobody serious claims we finish this tomorrow.

sources.label: Project Drawdown, ocean climate solutions, 2026.

claims.claim: It takes more energy to build a wind turbine than it ever produces
heard_as: solar panels never pay back their manufacturing
they only work because of subsidies
the carbon cost of building them cancels it out
claims.kernel: Making solar panels and turbines does produce carbon, and most of a turbine's lifetime emissions happen before it ever turns. That part is true.
claims.truth: The payback is quick. A solar panel makes up for its manufacturing emissions in four to eight months, then runs for 25 to 30 years. A wind turbine takes about seven months and runs for 20 to 25 years, with close to zero pollution once it's spinning. So a turbine spends **well over 95%** of its working life producing energy that is pure gain.
claims.say_this: A wind turbine pays back the carbon it took to build in about seven months, then keeps running for twenty-odd years.

pushback.if: What about when the wind isn't blowing
pushback.reply: That's a different question, and a fair one. It's about storage and grid design, rather than whether the turbine is worth building.

sources.label: United Nations, Climate Mythbusters.
ScienceDirect, wind turbine energy payback.

claims.claim: renewables and EVs mean a lot more mining
heard_as: Green energy needs way more mining
Renewables are just moving the mining
We'll destroy the planet with lithium mines
EVs need more resources than petrol cars
The mining for green tech is unsustainable
You're trading one extraction problem for another
claims.kernel: The pictures of lithium mines and cobalt operations in the news are real. Demand for battery minerals is going up, and new mines are being approved, sometimes amid controversy. If you compare a factory-made solar panel with a coal mine that is already running, renewables look like extra mining on top. What that comparison leaves out is the coal fed into a coal plant every single year, and the oil and gas that have to be extracted without end.
claims.truth: Per unit of electricity, coal is by far the most mining-hungry source: - Coal needs about **30 times more mining** than renewables per unit of electricity. - Coal needs about 100 times more mining than nuclear per unit. - Gas needs ongoing extraction of about 125,000 tonnes of gas for every TWh (terawatt-hour, a billion kilowatt-hours) of electricity. These figures already count the rock that gets moved, not only the useful metal. Copper makes up only 0.6% of its ore, so getting 1 kg of copper means digging up 160 kg of ore and moving 510 kg of rock. Fossil fuels go through the same calculation, and they come out worse. At the peak of the clean energy build-out, around 2040, solar, turbines, power lines and EVs will need about **25-50 million tonnes of minerals a year**. That sounds enormous, but it is a fraction of what fossil fuel extraction moves every year. The real difference is between a one-off need and a continuous one. Building a coal plant uses fewer raw materials than building a solar plant. But the coal plant then needs a constant supply of coal for its whole 40-year life. A solar panel or wind turbine, once built, needs no more materials, because its fuel (sunshine or wind) is free. Count both building and running, and solar, wind and nuclear all need far less mining in total than coal or gas. The picture also improves over time as technology gets more efficient: - The silver in a 2018 solar panel could now make 2 panels. - The silver in a 2010 panel could now make 5 panels. - Solar panels now use ⅛ of the polysilicon they needed in 2004. Electricity and cars tell slightly different stories. Mining for electricity falls as we move from coal to solar and wind. Mining for EVs on their own may rise a little compared with petrol cars. Put electricity and transport together, and total mining still falls by a wide margin.
claims.say_this: It's actually the other way round: going clean means less mining overall, not more. Coal power needs about 30 times more mining than renewables, and 100 times more than nuclear, for the same amount of electricity. Coal has to be dug up **continuously**, while solar panels and turbines only need their materials once, when they're built. We do need copper, lithium and nickel for clean tech, but the total amount of mining goes down.

pushback.if: Look at all these new lithium mines opening.
pushback.reply: They're opening because demand is growing fast. But the total amount of rock moved for the transition is still a fraction of what fossil fuel extraction moves. And once the new mines are running, they work for decades without the endless coal deliveries a coal plant depends on.

pushback.if: Coal mines already exist. Renewable mines are new.
pushback.reply: That framing hides the main point. Existing coal mines need constant new blasting, digging and transport. Their impact is never paid off: it carries on every day. A solar panel, once built, needs no more mining.

pushback.if: Watch out for those charts saying renewables need way more materials.
pushback.reply: Some do circulate, especially a 2015-era chart showing renewables needing more materials than fossil fuels. That chart is out of date (it predates the big efficiency gains in solar and wind) and usually leaves out the fuel burned in coal and gas plants, which is the largest material cost of fossil fuels.

pushback.if: EVs really do need more mining than petrol cars.
pushback.reply: For the car alone, roughly yes. But add up all the mining a petrol car needs over its life (steel, aluminium, and the oil pumped and refined) and compare it with an EV (steel, aluminium, battery), and the gap is smaller than it looks. Combine transport and electricity, and **total mining falls** a long way.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA, mineral intensity of electricity generation
Our World in Data, Mining and materials per unit energy

claims.claim: we need fossil fuels to build renewable energy
heard_as: You need oil to build solar panels
Wind turbines are made with fossil fuels
Renewables are just fossil fuels in disguise
It takes more energy to make a solar panel than it produces
Going green requires fossil fuels
Renewables can't reproduce themselves
claims.kernel: In the narrowest sense, it's true. Cement kilns, mining lorries and container ships still mostly run on fossil fuels, so a solar panel made today does carry a little fossil fuel inside it. When someone points that out and says "so renewables aren't really clean", the fact they start from is correct. It's the conclusion drawn from it that misleads.
claims.truth: There is a measure made for this question: **EROI (Energy Return on Investment)**. It compares how much energy a system gives back over its life with the energy that went into building it. - Solar panels take less than one year to pay back the energy used to build them. They then run for 25 to 30 years, producing roughly 25 times the energy it took to make them over their life. - Wind and nuclear take a few months to pay back, then run for decades. - An EROI below 1 means a system loses energy overall. Nothing on the modern grid comes anywhere near that. - An EROI of 5 or less is weak. Once waste is properly accounted for, solar, wind and nuclear all score well above 10, the level most experts treat as "good enough" to run a modern society. History helps here. **Every past energy transition** used the system of its day to build the next one. Timber-fired steam engines built the first coal mines. Coal-powered steelworks built the first oil rigs. Today, factories running on fossil fuels are building the machines that will replace them. This is what a transition looks like, not proof that it can't happen.
claims.say_this: Every energy transition has used the old system to build the new one, and that doesn't mean we're stuck with it. A solar panel pays back the energy used to make it in less than a year, then keeps running for 25 to 30 years, and wind and nuclear pay back in a few months. So yes, we use some fossil fuels to build renewables today, but it's a small, short-term energy debt with a very large payoff.

pushback.if: But mining and shipping are still fossil-fuel powered.
pushback.reply: That's right, and it's where the remaining work lies. Mining companies are already electrifying drills and heavy machinery, partly because it saves them money. Panel and turbine makers are moving to factories run on renewable power, for the same reason. So each new generation of renewables starts out cleaner than the last.

pushback.if: OK but the EROI numbers are still lower than for oil and coal at their peaks.
