pushback.reply: That's true for some historical fossil fuel comparisons, but there is an "energy cliff" to bear in mind. Above an EROI of about 10, extra gains barely matter for running a modern society. Solar, wind and nuclear all sit comfortably above that line, and the physics doesn't require us to chase the highest possible number.

pushback.if: So we'll always need some fossil fuel input.
pushback.reply: Yes, for a shrinking share and for a shrinking length of time. The fossil fuel left in supply chains falls every year as manufacturing itself runs on electricity. Nothing in physics locks it in.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Hall C., Prieto P., King C., and others. EROI research literature on solar, wind and nuclear systems

claims.claim: renewables aren't replacing fossil fuels, they're just being added on top
heard_as: Renewables are just being added on top
There's no energy transition, it's an addition
Fossil fuel use is still going up, so nothing has changed
The world isn't really moving off fossil fuels
Renewables can't scale
We keep adding wind and solar and it never makes a difference
The transition is a myth
claims.kernel: Look at a global chart of energy use and both fossil fuels and renewables are still rising. It really does look as if renewables are being added rather than replacing anything. In the poorest, fastest-growing economies, that is roughly what is happening today: total energy demand is rising, so both lines go up. When someone says "the energy transition is a myth", that chart looks like their evidence.
claims.truth: The global total hides three quite different situations: - **Energy addition** (stage 1): renewables are added on top and fossil fuels grow as normal. There are no clear real-world examples of this at country level today. - **Energy displacement** (stage 2): renewables cover demand that would otherwise have gone to fossil fuels. Fossil fuels still grow, but more slowly. China is the classic case. - **Energy transition** (stage 3): renewables replace fossil fuels, so fossil fuel use falls. Denmark, the UK and Finland are clear examples. More than half of the world's countries have already passed **"peak fossil fuels" in electricity**, even while their total electricity demand kept rising. - UK: fossil fuel electricity down by almost half since its peak in 2008. - Denmark: down by almost 80% since 2000. - Finland: down by more than two-thirds since 2000. - Worldwide in 2022, renewables supplied 92% of new electricity demand, and fossil fuels the remaining 8%. - Between 2010 and 2022, renewables supplied 57% of the growth in global electricity. Analysts now expect coal, oil and gas each to reach their global peak within the next five years. Sales of new petrol and diesel cars already peaked in 2017.
claims.say_this: In countries like the UK, Denmark and Finland, renewables are already replacing fossil fuels, and in China and much of the world they're covering new demand that would otherwise have gone to coal and gas. Almost nowhere are renewables simply added on top, and coal, oil and gas are each expected to peak worldwide within about five years.

pushback.if: But global fossil fuel use is still rising.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that is the true part of the claim. But the global total adds together countries at different stages. Most are at stage 2 (displacement) today and moving into stage 3 (transition), and at country level, transition is clearly gaining ground.

pushback.if: Renewables can only replace some of it.
pushback.reply: For most of the electricity system, they can do the heavy lifting. The last 20-30% of the grid and hard-to-clean industry need other tools: nuclear, hydro, geothermal, storage, and some gas as a shrinking backup. That is very different from saying renewables aren't replacing fossil fuels. They are, and the countries doing it show where others are heading.

pushback.if: You're cherry-picking Denmark.
pushback.reply: Denmark is ahead of the pack, but the pattern is common across Europe. The UK, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Ireland and Italy have all seen large falls in electricity from fossil fuels. Outside Europe, the US has moved more slowly, but its coal plants are now clearly in retreat. The transition looks different from place to place because countries started at different times with different resources, not because it isn't happening.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Ember, Global Electricity Review 2023
Our World in Data, Energy transition dashboard
IEA, Renewables 2023

claims.claim: solar panels and wind turbines create huge amounts of waste
heard_as: Wind blades can't be recycled
Solar panels are toxic waste
We're just creating a new landfill problem
Nobody knows what to do with old solar panels
Renewables produce huge amounts of e-waste
The environmental cost is being hidden
claims.kernel: There are real photos, and they get shared a lot. A heap of old wind blades or dumped solar panels in a field makes a vivid image. What the photo doesn't show is the coal ash lagoons that have sat outside coal plants for a century, or the oil sludge left by decades of drilling. The dumping site you can see is small next to the fossil fuel one you can't.
claims.truth: Waste per megawatt-hour (MWh) of electricity: | Source | kg per MWh | |---|---| | Coal | 89 | | Solar PV | 2 | | Wind | 0.2 | So coal creates about **50 times more waste than solar** and 500 times more than wind, for each unit of electricity. Here is the waste over 25 years for one average UK person, if all their electricity came from a single source, set against other kinds of waste they produce: | Source | Total waste (kg) | |---|---| | Municipal household waste | 12,100 | | Coal | 10,700 | | Plastic | 1,900 | | Electronic waste | 600 | | Solar PV | 200 | | Wind | 20 | Over 25 years, that person's coal waste would come to about 10 tonnes. Their solar waste would be 200 kg, and their wind waste 20 kg. How toxic the waste is matters too: - Wind turbines: 80-85% of their parts can be recycled. Blades are the difficult part. They are hard to recycle and often end up in landfill, but they are classed as non-hazardous in the US and Europe, so the health risk is low. - Solar panels: silicon panels contain small amounts of lead, and cadmium telluride panels contain traces of cadmium (about 0.1% of the panel's weight). Both are manageable at the end of a panel's life if panels are collected properly. - Coal ash: contains **mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium and chromium**, which are far more dangerous, and a coal plant produces it for as long as it runs. Switching from coal to renewables cuts both the amount of waste and how toxic it is.
claims.say_this: For the same amount of electricity, solar creates about 50 times less waste than coal, and wind about 500 times less. Renewables aren't waste-free, but the photos of dumped blades leave out the coal ash we've been piling up quietly for decades.

pushback.if: But wind blades are ending up in landfill.
pushback.reply: Some are, and the industry is working on it. Siemens and others now make recyclable blades, and several European governments have proposed banning turbine blades from landfill by the end of the decade. The amount is tiny compared with coal ash landfills, but being smaller than something worse is no reason to stop tackling it.

pushback.if: Solar panels are full of toxic materials.
pushback.reply: Silicon panels contain small amounts of lead (in the soldering), and cadmium telluride panels contain traces of cadmium. Both can be recovered and reused, and manufacturers already do this where old panels are collected properly. The toxicity issue is real, but it is well understood and manageable.

pushback.if: We haven't figured out recycling yet.
pushback.reply: The aluminium and glass in solar panels can already be recycled: they're the same main materials as in drinks cans and bottles. Recycling rates are still low in many countries, but most panels installed today have another 10-20 years of life ahead of them. That gives the industry time to build up recycling, and countries like Germany and Japan are already ahead.

claims.claim: solar and wind take up too much land
heard_as: Solar farms are ruining the countryside
Wind turbines are visual pollution
We can't afford to give up farmland for panels
The whole planet would need to be covered in solar
Renewables destroy wildlife habitat
There isn't enough land for renewables
claims.kernel: It's easy to make it look alarming in a photo. A field covered in solar panels, or a ridge lined with turbines, can feel like the countryside is being taken over, especially in countries that care deeply about their landscapes. What the photo can't show is how much power those panels make, or how much land coal and gas really use once mining, drilling and their infrastructure are counted.
claims.truth: Here is roughly how much land each source uses per unit of electricity, in square metres per MWh, including mining and the grid: | Source | m² per MWh | |---|---| | Nuclear | 0.3 | | Gas | 1 | | Solar (rooftop) | 3 | | Solar (ground, CdTe) | 13 | | Coal | 15 | | Solar (ground, silicon) | 19 | | Hydropower | 33 | - Nuclear is the most land-efficient way to make electricity. - Rooftop solar uses almost no new land, because it sits on buildings that already exist. - **Coal uses more land** than most solar farms once its mines and ash dumps are counted. - Hydropower is often the most land-hungry source, because reservoirs flood large areas. Wind is a special case. The land a turbine stands on directly is tiny, well under 0.1% of land even at large scale. Its visual footprint (all the area from which you can see turbines) would be 2-3% of the world's land if we got everything from wind. And land under turbines can still be farmed: crops and animals go right up to the base, and the farmer earns extra income from the power. If the whole world ran on a single source, in theory it would need: - Nuclear: less than 0.01% of land - Wind (direct footprint): less than 0.1% of land - Solar: about 0.5% of land - Wind (visual footprint): 2-3%, rising to 10-15% in small, crowded countries Some country examples: - The US could decarbonise with 1-6% of its land under solar and a wind visual footprint of 5-22%. - The EU could reach net zero with 3% of its land under solar and a wind visual footprint of up to 15%. Just **1% of land as solar** would already cover the EU's electricity demand today. - South Korea and Singapore really are too small and dense for a path based only on renewables. They are rare exceptions, not the rule.
claims.say_this: They need some land, but much less than people think: powering the whole world with solar would take about 0.5% of the world's land, compared with the half of habitable land we already use for farming. Apart from tiny crowded places like Singapore, it's a manageable share.

pushback.if: But the photos of fields of solar panels look terrible.
pushback.reply: It depends what you compare them with. The US uses **2.5% of its land** to grow crops for bioethanol, an area the size of the UK, and that covers only 10% of the country's petrol needs. The same land under solar would produce enough electricity to power the entire US two to three times over. Nobody worries about the bioethanol land because it looks like an ordinary maize field.

pushback.if: Rural people don't want turbines in their view.
pushback.reply: That's a fair concern. What helps is fair partnership with local communities: projects they co-own, cheaper electricity for people who live nearby, and open, transparent decisions on where turbines go. Where communities share the benefits, opposition drops. Where distant developers impose projects with nothing in it for local people, opposition is fierce.

pushback.if: We're taking farmland for panels.
pushback.reply: Some farmland is being converted, but it's a small share of the total. Many large solar farms are deliberately placed on poorer land, brownfield sites and old industrial land. Rooftops and car parks can take a big share of demand without touching farmland at all.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
Our World in Data, Land use per unit of energy

claims.claim: renewable energy is too expensive
heard_as: Renewables are only cheap because of subsidies
Solar doesn't work without government handouts
Once you factor in storage, it's not cheap
Fossil fuels are still cheaper
Nobody would build solar without incentives
It only works when the sun shines
claims.kernel: For decades it was true. Solar panels used to be a niche product for enthusiasts, wind turbines needed subsidies, and fossil fuels were clearly cheaper. Anyone whose picture of energy comes from the debates of the 2000s is remembering correctly. What changed is that between about 2010 and 2020, the cost of solar fell by about 85% and wind roughly halved, and the order flipped.
claims.truth: - Solar costs have fallen **tenfold** since 2010, with a drop of about 85% in the last decade alone. Analysts expect a further 50% fall by 2030. - In 2023, 96% of new solar and onshore wind projects were cheaper than building a new coal or gas plant. - Three-quarters of new solar and wind projects were cheaper even than fossil fuel plants that were already built and running. - In Australia, solar plus batteries is about 30% cheaper than gas plants used at times of peak demand. - In India, solar plus batteries is already cheaper than many existing fossil fuel plants. - More than a quarter of global emissions are now covered by some kind of carbon tax or emissions trading scheme. Renewables get cheaper because of the **learning curve**: each time installed capacity has doubled, costs have historically fallen by 20-30%. Fossil fuels don't follow a learning curve. Their prices swing with world events, but they show no long-term fall. Fossil fuels also carry hidden costs that don't appear on the bill: - Air pollution: burning coal, oil and gas causes an estimated $6 trillion a year in damage worldwide, through heart disease, cancer, stroke and lung illness, and millions of early deaths each year. - Climate damage: not included in the price of fossil fuels, but paid by future generations and poorer countries.
claims.say_this: That was true 15 years ago, but it stopped being true around 2015: today solar and wind are cheaper than new coal or gas almost everywhere, and often cheaper than fossil fuel plants that are already running. Fossil fuels only look cheap because their air pollution alone costs almost $6 trillion a year worldwide and kills millions of people.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are only cheap because of subsidies.
pushback.reply: That was true 15 years ago, but not any more. Subsidies helped renewables close the gap when they were expensive. Today they're cheap because they are made at **huge scale**. Compare the price of new solar in a competitive auction with new gas, and solar wins without subsidy in most markets.

pushback.if: When you add batteries, it's not cheap any more.
pushback.reply: Batteries do add cost, and they're needed to cover the times when the sun isn't shining or the wind isn't blowing. But in Australia, solar plus batteries is already cheaper than gas at peak times. Battery costs are following the same learning curve solar did, falling about 90% over the past decade. In most places, the full system still comes out cheaper.

pushback.if: Fossil fuels look cheap in my energy bill.
pushback.reply: That's because your bill doesn't include the deaths from air pollution, the healthcare costs or the climate damage. Those costs are real. They're simply paid by other people, mostly poorer people and future generations. That is what "hidden cost" means.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs
Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy Analysis

claims.claim: we're going to run out of the minerals needed for clean energy
heard_as: We're running out of lithium
There's not enough cobalt in the world
Green energy will hit resource limits
Rare earths are running out
You can't scale renewables because of minerals
Peak lithium is coming
claims.kernel: "We're running out of X" is an old worry. It has come and gone for oil, water and food, and now it's the turn of minerals: every generation gets its own "peak resource" story. And the clean energy build-out does need a lot of particular minerals in a short time. Anyone who reads a headline about lithium shortages is right that supply is tight. The mistake is to confuse a short-term bottleneck in getting minerals out with a long-term lack of reserves.
claims.truth: Reserves are growing faster than production: - Global lithium production went from about 30,000-40,000 tonnes a year in 2008 to over 150,000 tonnes a year by 2022. - Global lithium reserves went from a few million tonnes in 2008 to **over 20 million tonnes** by 2022. Clean energy technology would raise overall demand for materials by **5-15%**, which is far from a runaway increase. Supplies will be tighter for some materials, mainly lithium, cobalt and copper. Even for these, there is either enough today or the gap is closing through new deposits, using other materials instead, and using less of them. Efficiency is already improving fast: - The silver in a 2018 solar panel could now make 2 panels. - The silver in a 2010 panel could now make 5 panels. - Solar panels use ⅛ of the polysilicon they needed in 2004. Two words that often get mixed up: - Reserves: deposits that can be mined at a profit with today's technology. - Resources: all known deposits, including ones that aren't yet worth mining. Both grow as prices change and technology improves. The major energy agencies agree: - IEA: generally no signs of shortages in available resources. - IRENA: no scarcity of reserves for energy transition minerals, and reserves that can be mined at a profit have grown. - Energy Transitions Commission: no fundamental shortage of any raw material for a global net-zero transition. - Rocky Mountain Institute: the world has enough minerals for the entire energy transition and is building the mines quickly.
claims.say_this: We're not running out: lithium reserves have grown faster than lithium production, and the IEA, IRENA, the Rocky Mountain Institute and the Energy Transitions Commission all say there's no fundamental shortage. The real risk is getting the minerals out of the ground fast enough over the next 5 to 10 years, because opening a new mine takes about a decade.

pushback.if: But mining takes forever to open.
pushback.reply: That's right, and it is the real bottleneck. Finding and exploring a new deposit takes **over a decade**. Sourcing lithium takes about 4 years in Australia and about 6 years in South America. Once a deposit is found, permits and construction take about 5 more years, and in the US the permits alone take 7 to 10 years. That is why the next 5-10 years are the tight period, and geology has little to do with it.

pushback.if: We're already fighting over lithium.
pushback.reply: Prices jump around because the industry is growing quickly, but volatile prices aren't the same as scarcity. Even a big spike in the lithium price doesn't mean the world is running out. It means demand outran production for a while. New reserves are being found all the time.

pushback.if: What about after 2030?
pushback.reply: Swapping materials and recycling ease the pressure over time. Tesla now uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which contain no cobalt, in more than half its cars. BYD is investing in sodium-ion batteries, which use no cobalt or lithium at all. Aluminium can replace copper in power lines when copper gets expensive. The 2030s look easier for materials than the 2020s.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)
IEA, Critical Minerals reports
IRENA, Energy Transition Minerals reports
Energy Transitions Commission, Making Mission Possible
Rocky Mountain Institute, Reality Check on Clean Energy Minerals

claims.claim: This is all fine for people who can afford it
heard_as: electric cars are for rich people
green policies hit the poorest hardest
easy to be green on a big salary
claims.kernel: This is largely correct, and it's worth saying so straight away. New EVs, heat pumps, home retrofits and organic food all cost money upfront. Climate policy designed carelessly does land hardest on the people with the least, and that is how it loses public support.
claims.truth: None of this is a reason to do less. The people with the smallest footprints are already the poorest, and they are also hit first and hardest by heatwaves, flooding and sudden jumps in energy prices, so carrying on as we are isn't neutral either. Ireland's Climate Change Advisory Council made this point in 2026: depending on fossil fuels is what leaves households exposed to price shocks, and the Council called for investment in public transport and a fair move to EVs. The answer lies in how policy is designed (grants, retrofit schemes, public transport, and taxing the highest emitters) rather than in giving up on the goal.
claims.say_this: You're right, and that's a reason to design this properly, not to drop it. The people with the smallest footprints are already the ones being hit first.

pushback.if: Politicians never design it properly
pushback.reply: Often that's true, and it's exactly what to campaign on, because the alternative on offer is price shocks from fossil fuels we don't control.

sources.label: RTE, CCAC 2026 Annual Review.

claims.claim: wind farms kill huge numbers of birds
heard_as: Wind turbines are bird murder machines
Wind farms destroy migrating birds
Trump was right about windmills killing birds
Bats are being wiped out by turbines
Wind farms are ecological disasters
Turbines kill more birds than we're told
claims.kernel: It's easy to picture, and there's a real problem inside it. Turbines do kill birds, and videos of eagles hitting blades are horrible to watch. Some species, such as birds of prey and migrating birds, really are at higher risk. The RSPB, a charity set up to protect birds, has raised concerns about specific wind farms. So the worry isn't made up. The question is how big it is compared with everything else that kills birds.
claims.truth: Birds killed each year in the US, by cause: | Cause | Birds killed per year | |---|---| | Cats | 2.4 billion | | Buildings (windows) | 600 million | | Cars | 200 million | | Pesticides | 67 million | | Power lines | 28 million | | Phone/comms towers | 6.6 million | | Wind turbines | 1.2 million | Wind turbines kill about **2,000 times fewer birds than cats**, and far fewer than cars, buildings or pesticides. Per turbine, on average: - Each turbine kills 4-18 birds a year. - Each turbine kills 6-20 bats a year. As a share of their population, bats are more at risk than birds. Some birds are much more affected than others: - Birds of prey (eagles, hawks) use hilltops to catch the wind, which is exactly where wind farms tend to be built. - Migrating birds are at higher risk when turbines sit on their route. - Losing rare or endangered birds matters more than losing common ones, and a comparison based only on numbers misses that.
claims.say_this: Wind turbines do kill some birds, about 1.2 million a year in the US, but cats kill 2.4 billion, buildings 600 million and cars 200 million. And simple fixes, like painting one blade black or stopping turbines in very low wind, cut those deaths sharply for almost no cost.

pushback.if: Trump was right when he said windmills kill all the birds.
pushback.reply: "All the birds" is plainly wrong. Each year in the US, turbines kill about 0.05% of the number of birds cats kill. The RSPB, a charity set up to protect birds, has built its own turbine to power its headquarters. That's not what an organisation does if it thinks turbines are a disaster for birds.

pushback.if: But it's the wrong birds, eagles and raptors.
pushback.reply: That's right, and that risk is real, which is why targeted fixes matter. These cut deaths of birds of prey and bats without losing much energy: - **Stop turbines in low wind.** Bats struggle to fly in stronger wind, so most bat strikes happen below 5-6 m/s. A Pennsylvania study found bat deaths fell 44% with a cut-off at 5 m/s, and 93% with a cut-off at 6.5 m/s. The loss of energy was tiny. - **Paint one blade black.** A Norwegian test cut bird deaths by more than 70%, and no white-tailed eagles were killed after the blades were painted. - **Play high-pitched sounds** to warn bats away. A trial in Texas cut deaths of two bat species by 54% and 78%. - **Track eagles by GPS** near turbines, with turbines shutting down automatically when an eagle comes close. - **An Australian wind farm** cut bird deaths by 54% while losing only 0.1% of its income. - **In Cadiz, Spain,** bird deaths halved for a loss of only 0.07% of energy output.

pushback.if: Climate change harms birds too.
pushback.reply: Very much so. Fossil fuels harm birds through climate change, air pollution, oil spills, run-off from coal mines and acid rain. If you care about bird numbers, the fossil fuel system does far more harm than the wind farms replacing it.
